sections.intro: From the Blitz PPL mock oral. Dave opens with a ramp check; Steve likes hearing the reg number. Mike (11/17): fast paced, oral just under an hour, no trick questions besides stalls, and he won’t let you dig yourself into a hole.
qs: Ramp check: what documents must you have to fly? (Opening question)

For a typical private pilot airplane flight, have your appropriate pilot certificate, an acceptable government-issued photo ID, and a valid medical certificate when required, in your physical possession or readily accessible in the aircraft. If operating under BasicMed, meet its eligibility, documentation, and operating requirements instead of assuming a medical certificate is required. Reference: 61.3 and 61.23. For student solo flight, also have the required instructor endorsements for the aircraft and operation, including a current solo endorsement and any required cross-country authorizations. A student must carry the logbook with required endorsements on solo cross-country flights; carrying a logbook is not a blanket requirement for every local solo or ordinary private pilot flight. Reference: 61.51(i), 61.87, and 61.93. Distinguish pilot documents from aircraft documents: check the aircraft’s airworthiness certificate, registration, applicable operating limitations/approved flight manual and supplements, and current weight-and-balance data. A radio station license is generally relevant to international operations. Aircraft documents are covered again in Question 17.
Logbook and IACRA review: is everything logged and endorsed?

Ground training logged (or school records), all solo and checkride endorsements. Gouges: one applicant had no ground training logged and had to call the instructor; another was missing an earlier solo endorsement. Check everything before the checkride.
What class of medical certificate is required for your license?

For ordinary private pilot airplane privileges, at least a third-class medical is the usual medical certificate. Eligible pilots may instead operate under BasicMed within its requirements and limitations. A first-time student cannot simply use BasicMed without meeting its prior-medical requirements.
What is the duration of that class of medical certificate ?

For private pilot privileges, a third-class medical lasts through the end of the 60th calendar month after the examination month if you were under 40 on the examination date, or the 24th calendar month if 40 or older. Age at the examination controls. A special issuance may impose a shorter duration.
Can a drug or alcohol conviction (not related to aviation activities) affect your pilot privileges ?

Yes. Specified drug convictions can support certificate denial, suspension, or revocation. Alcohol-related motor vehicle actions also trigger FAA reporting requirements; report each qualifying action within 60 days under 61.15, separately from medical application disclosures. A second qualifying motor vehicle action within three years can create additional certificate consequences.
Refusal to submit to a blood alcohol test is grounds for what ?

Refusing a qualifying alcohol test, or refusing to provide or authorize release of required results, can support denial of an application for a certificate, rating, or authorization for up to one year and suspension or revocation of an existing certificate, rating, or authorization. This concerns tests and requests covered by the regulation.
Are you required to have a periodic flight review? What kind? How often ?

Normally, to act as PIC you need a flight review within the preceding 24 calendar months. It includes at least one hour of ground and one hour of flight training, plus an instructor endorsement of satisfactory completion. Qualifying practical tests, proficiency checks, or FAA WINGS phases can substitute as specified.
What are the recency of flight experience requirements to carry passengers ?

Normally, to carry passengers you need three takeoffs and landings in the preceding 90 days, as sole manipulator, in the appropriate category, class, and type if required. Tailwheel landings must be full stop. For passenger carriage from one hour after sunset to one hour before sunrise, three qualifying full-stop night takeoffs and landings are required. Gouge: Day: 3 takeoffs and landings in the preceding 90 days (full stop in a tailwheel). Night: 3 takeoffs and landings to a full stop from 1 hr after sunset to 1 hr before sunrise. Flight review every 24 calendar months.
How long after a change of address do you have to notify the FAA ?

Notify the FAA of a permanent mailing address change within 30 days. After that period, you may not exercise certificate privileges until you provide the required notification. Updating a driver's license or a school account does not update the FAA record.
When may a private pilot accept money for flying an aircraft?

A private pilot generally cannot act as PIC for compensation or hire. A common exception permits sharing only fuel, oil, airport expenditures, and rental fees while paying at least your pro rata share; the flight must also meet applicable common-purpose guidance. Other narrow exceptions exist, including incidental business flying when no passengers or property are carried for compensation or hire. Gouge: No compensation or hire; may share operating expenses (fuel, oil, airport fees, rental) pro rata with passengers with a common purpose. Exceptions in 61.113(c)–(i). Mike: scenario: he offers to pay you to fly him to a baseball game. Can you? No: no compensation or hire; you could only share expenses pro rata with a common purpose. Steve: opens with “you’re a private pilot, what can and can’t you do?”
May a student pilot log pilot in command time?

Yes. A student pilot may log PIC when sole occupant, appropriately endorsed for the flight, and undergoing training for a pilot certificate or rating. An instructor's presence does not let an otherwise unrated student log PIC merely because the student manipulates the controls.
What actions are you required to take prior to takeoff?

Become familiar with all available information concerning the flight. Review weather, fuel, runway lengths and performance, aircraft condition, weight and balance, NOTAMs, airspace restrictions, and suitable alternatives. For flights away from the airport vicinity, 91.103 specifically includes weather reports and forecasts, fuel, alternatives, and known ATC delays. Complete the aircraft checklist and passenger briefing.
You drank a beer late last night, and a friend wants to go flying early this morning. Is this a problem? Why or why not?

Possibly. At least eight hours must pass after drinking, but eight hours alone does not make the flight legal or safe. You must also be free of alcohol's influence, below the prohibited concentration, and physically fit. A hangover, dehydration, or poor sleep can justify canceling even when the time requirement is met.
What is the blood alcohol limit for pilots?

You may not serve as a crewmember with an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater in blood or breath as defined by the rule. You also may not serve within eight hours of drinking or while under the influence. A concentration below 0.04 does not excuse impairment.

You and two friends flew to Key West for the day. Upon meeting for the return flight, you find that one of your passengers is quite drunk. Your other passenger says No problem, he always sleeps it off on the way back. Is he right?

No. Except in an emergency, you may not allow a person who appears intoxicated, or shows physical indications of being under the influence of drugs, to be carried. The rule has a separate exception for a medical patient under proper care. Sleeping during the flight does not make an intoxicated passenger acceptable.
Can you drop objects from your aircraft?

Yes, if reasonable precautions prevent injury or damage to persons or property. You may not allow an object to be dropped in a way that creates a hazard. Also consider local restrictions, aircraft limitations, and the general prohibition on careless or reckless operation.

For VFR in an airplane, considering wind and forecast weather, carry enough fuel to reach the first intended landing and then fly at normal cruising speed for at least 30 minutes by day or 45 minutes at night. These are departure planning minimums, not sensible targets for arriving nearly empty. Gouge: POH fuel flow at the planned power setting; day VFR reserve 30 min, night 45 min. Mike (11/17): point to fuel used on the nav log, and the daytime VFR fuel requirement.
What is Mode C? Where is it required?
Altitude reporting with your transponder. Required in Class A, B and C; above Class B/C up to 10,000; at or above 10,000 MSL except at or below 2,500 AGL; in the Mode C veil.
What is the Mode C veil?
30 nm around the primary Class B airport, surface to 10,000 MSL.
Generally the same airspace as Mode C: A, B, C, the veil, above B/C, and at or above 10,000 MSL except at or below 2,500 AGL.
What documents are required to be in the aircraft? (SPARROW)

SPARROW: Supplements, Placards, Airworthiness certificate, Radio station license (international only), Registration, Operating limitations, Weight and balance. ARROW is the shorter version: airworthiness certificate, registration, radio station license when required for international operations, operating limitations/approved AFM or applicable POH and supplements, and current weight-and-balance information as applicable to the aircraft's approved operating data. Not every letter is an identical standalone document requirement. The airworthiness certificate must be displayed as required. Gouge: On you: pilot certificate, medical (or BasicMed docs), government photo ID. In the airplane: SPARROW (above).
What documents are required to be on your person?

Carry or have readily accessible the appropriate pilot certificate, acceptable government photo ID, and medical certificate when required. BasicMed has different document provisions. Student pilots need applicable endorsements, and solo cross-country flights have specific logbook-carrying requirements. A certificated private pilot generally does not have to carry a personal logbook on an ordinary domestic flight.
What documents must be kept, but not necessarily in the aircraft or on your person?

Keep pilot training, experience, and endorsement records needed to establish qualification and currency. Aircraft maintenance records establish inspection status, AD compliance, life-limited part status, alterations, and maintenance approval. They normally stay safely on the ground. Review the different retention requirements in 91.417; not every maintenance entry has the same retention period.
When is supplemental oxygen required for the crew? (At 16,500 ft, do you need anything?)
Above 12,500 to 14,000 MSL: crew after 30 min. Above 14,000: crew the whole time. So at 16,500, yes.
When must passengers be provided oxygen?
Above 15,000 MSL each occupant must be provided oxygen (they don’t have to use it).
What equipment is required to be installed in the aircraft for flight, VFR day? VFR night?

Day VFR equipment under 91.205(b) includes airspeed, altimeter, magnetic direction indicator, applicable engine gauges, fuel quantity for each tank, required landing-gear indication, applicable anticollision lighting, restraints, and applicable flotation/signaling equipment for certain overwater operations. Night adds position lights, anticollision lights, adequate electrical energy, required accessible spare fuses, and a landing light if operated for hire. Also check type design, equipment lists, ADs, and other applicable rules; a mnemonic is not the whole airworthiness decision. Steve: 91.203 and 91.205. Oil temp gauge inop: can you placard it and go? No; anything in ATOMATOFLAMES (and FLAPS at night) can’t be inoperative.
What is an ELT? What aircraft must have one?

The source appears to mean ELT: emergency locator transmitter. It transmits a distress signal after activation. Most U.S.-registered civil airplanes need an approved automatic ELT, but 91.207 lists exceptions and limited operations allowed with an inoperative or removed unit. Know the equipment installed and the exact exception before using one.
If an ELT is installed, the battery must be replaced/recharged if...?

Replace or recharge the ELT battery after more than one cumulative hour of transmitter use or when 50 percent of its useful life, or rechargeable useful charge life, has expired, as established by the manufacturer. The useful-life provision has an exception for batteries essentially unaffected during probable storage intervals.
Where must the ELT battery expiration date be posted?

The new replacement/recharge expiration date must be legibly marked on the outside of the transmitter and entered in the aircraft maintenance record. Do not confuse that battery date with the separate 12-calendar-month ELT inspection.
Are private pilots permitted to conduct formation flights?

Yes, with prior arrangement among the PICs of the aircraft involved. Formation flight is prohibited while carrying passengers for hire. Appropriate formation training, briefing, and collision-avoidance procedures are essential; agreement alone does not establish proficiency.
Describe the rule governing the right of way for: a. Aircraft in distress b. Converging aircraft c. Overtaking d. Landing

Aircraft in distress have priority. For same-category converging aircraft, the aircraft to the other's right has right of way; different-category priorities also apply. An overtaking aircraft gives way and passes well clear to the right. Aircraft on final or landing have priority, but a lower aircraft cannot cut in front of or overtake one on final.
What speed limits apply to propeller driven aircraft?

These general limits are not specific to propeller aircraft: below 10,000 MSL, generally 250 KIAS; at or below 2,500 AGL within four NM of a Class C/D primary airport, generally 200 KIAS; under Class B shelves or in a designated VFR corridor through Class B, 200 KIAS. Aircraft minimum-safe-speed provisions and authorizations may apply.
When and where is aerobatic flight permitted or prohibited?

Aerobatic flight is prohibited over congested areas, open-air assemblies, within Class B/C/D/E surface areas designated for an airport, within four NM of a Federal airway centerline, below 1,500 AGL, or with visibility under three SM. Aircraft limitations and parachute requirements also matter. With a non-crewmember aboard, exceeding 60 degrees bank or 30 degrees pitch generally requires approved parachutes, subject to listed exceptions.
Describe aircraft position lights (which color is where on the aircraft?)

Red is on the left wingtip, green on the right, and white faces aft. Their arrangement helps another pilot determine relative heading. Learn how the visible combination changes when you see an airplane approaching, crossing, or moving away.
When must the position lights be on? The anticollision lights?

Position lights are required from sunset to sunrise, subject to the rule's provisions. An aircraft equipped with an anticollision system normally operates with it on; the PIC may turn it off when operating conditions make doing so safer, such as distracting reflection in clouds or strobes affecting nearby pilots.

Your radios have failed while on downwind at a tower-controlled airport. The tower begins using light signals to communicate with you. What is the meaning of a steady red? Flashing red? Steady green? Flashing green?

In flight: steady green means cleared to land; flashing green means return for landing, with landing clearance to follow; steady red means give way to other aircraft and continue circling; flashing red means airport unsafe, do not land. Rock wings by day or use the prescribed light acknowledgment at night when practical.

You have successfully landed without radios. The tower continues to use light signals. What is the meaning of a steady red? Flashing red? Flashing green? Steady green? Alternating red and green? Flashing white?

On the ground: steady green means cleared for takeoff; flashing green means cleared to taxi; steady red means stop; flashing red means taxi clear of the runway in use; flashing white means return to the starting point on the airport. Alternating red/green means exercise extreme caution, both airborne and on the ground.
Describe the rules regarding the minimum altitude at which you may fly.

Except when necessary for takeoff/landing, always maintain altitude allowing an emergency landing without undue hazard after power loss. Over congested areas, stay at least 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within 2,000 feet horizontally. Elsewhere, normally remain at least 500 feet above the surface; over open water or sparsely populated areas stay at least 500 feet from people, vessels, vehicles, and structures.
When is a flight plan required (VFR)?

An ordinary domestic VFR flight generally does not require a filed VFR flight plan. ADIZ operations, certain special airspace procedures, and international flights can impose flight-plan requirements. A voluntary VFR flight plan supports search and rescue only when activated, monitored for overdue status, and properly closed; flight following is a different service. Mike: how do you file (and open/close) a VFR flight plan?
Currency = meeting the legal minimums (61.56, 61.57). Proficiency = actually being able to fly the airplane safely; it can take much more than the legal minimum.

sections.intro: From the Blitz PPL mock oral, plus gouge questions: Steve goes straight to Class G minimums and asks about a restricted area on the route.
qs: Class A: where is it and what do you need?
18,000 MSL to FL600. IFR only: instrument rating, IFR clearance, transponder and ADS-B.
Class B: chart depiction, entry and VFR minimums?
Solid blue. Explicit ATC clearance; Mode C and ADS-B. 3 sm, clear of clouds.
Class C: chart depiction, entry and VFR minimums?
Solid magenta. Two-way radio communication before entering; Mode C and ADS-B. 3 sm, 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal.
Class D: chart depiction, entry and VFR minimums?
Dashed blue. Two-way radio communication before entering. 3 sm, 500/1,000/2,000.
Class E: chart depiction and VFR minimums?
Dashed magenta (surface), magenta shading (700 AGL), blue shading (1,200 AGL). No entry requirement. Below 10,000: 3 sm, 500/1,000/2,000. At/above 10,000: 5 sm, 1,000/1,000/1 sm.
Not used in the United States.
Class G: what is it and what are the VFR minimums?

Uncontrolled. At or below 1,200 AGL: day 1 sm clear of clouds; night 3 sm, 500/1,000/2,000. Above 1,200 AGL below 10,000: day 1 sm 500/1,000/2,000; night 3 sm. At/above 10,000 and above 1,200 AGL: 5 sm, 1,000/1,000/1 sm.
Hazardous activity from 3 nm out from the U.S. coast. Check activity and avoid.
What is a restricted area? Can you enter?
Hazardous, often invisible activity. Entry when active needs permission from the controlling agency.
Flight prohibited without authorization (e.g. P-56 over the White House).
What is an MOA? Can you fly through?
Military operations area. VFR may enter without clearance; check activity and use caution.
What is a special flight rules area (SFRA)?
Airspace with special procedures in 14 CFR Part 93 (e.g. Grand Canyon, Washington DC). Read the requirements before flying there.
A passage through Class B without entering it; follow the published limits.
What is special VFR and when would you use it?
An ATC clearance to operate VFR in the surface area of controlled airspace below basic VFR minimums, below 10,000 MSL: 1 sm and clear of clouds.
How do you get a special VFR clearance?
Request it from ATC (tower, or approach/center if no tower).
Special VFR hazards and night rules?
Low visibility and terrain/obstacle risk. At night you need an instrument rating and an IFR-equipped airplane.
What are the VFR cruising altitudes?

In level cruising flight more than 3,000 feet above the surface, use magnetic course: 000-179 degrees uses odd thousands plus 500 feet; 180-359 uses even thousands plus 500, unless otherwise authorized by ATC or another listed exception applies. Course, not heading, determines the hemisphere. Terrain and cloud clearance still control.
What inspections are required on your aircraft? How often? Where are they recorded? (AAV1ATE)

For a typical training airplane, check the annual, applicable 100-hour inspections, AD compliance, ELT inspection/battery, transponder test, and any required altimeter/static/encoder tests. VOR checks apply when using VOR under IFR. Inspect maintenance records for actual dates, time-in-service limits, signatures, and return-to-service approvals. The annual is due every 12 calendar months; the 100-hour requirement depends on use. Gouge: AAV1ATE: Airworthiness directives, Annual (12 cal months), VOR check (30 days, IFR), 100-hour (for hire or flight instruction in an airplane you provide), Altimeter and pitot-static (24 cal months, IFR in controlled airspace), Transponder (24 cal months), ELT (12 cal months, battery). Mike: starts by going through your logbook and the aircraft maintenance books to make sure everything is up to date. Mike: gouge: ELT inspection wasn’t logged correctly so the airplane wasn’t airworthy; had to call the mechanic. He has you show airworthiness from the maintenance folder (ELT battery, transponder). Mike (11/17): go through AAV1ATE in the maintenance binder: which recurring ADs are there and which have been checked?
Does a transponder require calibration? When?

Yes. A required transponder must have been tested and inspected within the preceding 24 calendar months. Additional testing can be required following installation or maintenance where data correspondence error could be introduced. An aircraft's annual inspection does not automatically establish transponder compliance.
What other devices which operate with the transponder must be calibrated?

For controlled-airspace IFR operations, the static pressure system, each altimeter, and each automatic pressure-altitude reporting system must meet the 24-calendar-month test requirement. Additional tests follow certain system openings, installations, or maintenance. This complete IFR testing requirement is not automatically imposed on every VFR-only airplane just because it carries a transponder.
Ground NDB transmits; the ADF needle points to the station.
Ground station transmits radials; receiver shows your radial and course deviation.
VOR co-located with military TACAN; civil aircraft get VOR plus DME.
DME: what does it give you?
Discontinued in the U.S.; no longer used for navigation.
Point out each of the above on a sectional chart.

Use the current sectional legend: NDBs use a dotted circular symbol; VORs a hexagonal symbol; VOR/DME and VORTAC have their own composite symbols. Read the facility box for name, frequency, identifier, and associated information. A real chart is needed to point out actual examples; none was supplied. LORAN chains are a historical subject, not a present sectional navigation task.

What stations have Morse code identifiers on them? How do you find out what the identifier is for a particular station? What do you as a pilot have to do to your radios to hear the Morse code identifier?

VORs, NDBs, localizers, and associated distance facilities use identifiers as applicable. Obtain the expected identifier from the chart or approved navigation database. Tune the correct frequency, select the navigation audio on the audio panel, adjust identification/volume controls, and compare the received identifier. Approved decoded identification can be used when supported by the installed system and procedures.

The FAA has found the XYZ VOR to be out of adjustment and providing dangerously inaccurate guidance. Their maintenance men are working on the station now. How can you, the pilot, tell that the signals are not reliable?

Check NOTAMs and facility status. A station under maintenance may have its identification removed or transmit a test identification, and the cockpit may show a warning flag. A moving CDI or apparently sensible bearing alone does not prove reliable service. Do not use a facility reported out of service simply because it appears to work.
What is an FSS and how do you find one on the sectional?
Flight Service Station: briefings, flight plans, in-flight services. Find frequencies above the VOR box or in the Chart Supplement.
How can FSS help in flight, and on what frequencies?
Weather updates, flight plan open/close/changes, PIREPs, emergencies. Frequencies on the VOR box, 122.2, or remote outlets in the Chart Supplement.
What is Flight Watch? On what frequency?

Flight Watch was the En Route Flight Advisory Service, commonly contacted on 122.0 MHz. The dedicated service was discontinued in 2015. Use current published Flight Service frequencies and other approved weather sources instead; do not plan on receiving Flight Watch on 122.0.

An RCO is a Remote Communications Outlet. It extends access to Flight Service using a remotely located transmitter/receiver. The charted frequency and any transmit-only/receive-only notation determine how to set up your radios.
When might you transmit to the FSS on one frequency and receive on another?

A published arrangement may have you transmit on 122.1 MHz while listening to Flight Service through a VOR's voice channel. Tune the VOR on a navigation receiver, enable its voice audio, and transmit on the published communications frequency. Confirm that the current chart actually supports that arrangement and identify the receiving facility in your call.
What is a Transcribed Weather Broadcast? Where can you listen to one?

TWEB was a recorded weather broadcast service, historically available over selected navigation facilities. It is obsolete for present U.S. planning; Alaska TWEB ended in 2020. HIWAS also ended in the contiguous U.S. in 2020.
What is a VHF steer? When would you want one? Who gives it to you?

A VHF steer was direction-finding assistance based on your radio transmissions, historically provided by suitably equipped ground facilities to help an uncertain or lost pilot. Do not assume it is available today. Request assistance from ATC or Flight Service; give your position estimate, altitude, fuel, and situation, and use radar/GPS assistance when available.
What is radar? What does it do for you?

Primary radar detects reflected energy from targets; secondary surveillance obtains replies from aircraft transponders. ATC uses surveillance to support identification, traffic services, vectors, and separation appropriate to the airspace and flight rules. ADS-B is another surveillance source. Radar coverage and target detection are not universal, and a basic transponder does not itself detect other aircraft.
Describe VFR Flight Following: what it is, who does it, what its limitations are, how to get it.

VFR flight following is workload-permitting radar traffic advisory service, generally from approach control or center. Request it with callsign, type, position, altitude, and destination; follow the assigned squawk and instructions. It can provide traffic alerts and assistance, but does not replace see-and-avoid, VFR cloud clearance, or separate Class B entry authorization.
Does the airworthiness certificate expire? What about the registration?

Standard airworthiness certificate stays valid as long as maintenance, preventive maintenance and alterations follow Parts 43 and 91 and the airplane stays U.S. registered. Registration must be renewed every 7 years.
Which airspace will you fly through on your cross-country?
Walk the route on the sectional: classes, altitudes, special use airspace, requirements for each.

≤1,200 AGL: day 1 sm clear of clouds; night 3 sm 500/1,000/2,000 (1 sm clear of clouds in the pattern within ½ mi of the runway). >1,200 AGL <10,000 MSL: day 1 sm 500/1,000/2,000; night 3 sm. ≥10,000 MSL and >1,200 AGL: 5 sm, 1,000/1,000/1 sm. Steve: VFR minimums KOGD → KBMC: B, D and E.
Restricted area on your route: can you enter? Who do you contact?

Only if it’s not active or the controlling agency authorizes it. Find the controlling agency on the back of the sectional (special use airspace table): e.g. “SLC TRACON” = Salt Lake City Approach (terminal radar approach control). Steve: answer no, but acknowledge 91.3 emergency authority.
(Shows a TFR on the sectional.) What is it? Can you fly in it?
Temporary flight restriction; check the NOTAM for times, altitudes and who may enter. Generally no unless the NOTAM allows.
Special flight rules over the Grand Canyon: what are they? Can you fly over it?
Grand Canyon SFRA (14 CFR Part 93 Subpart U / SFAR 50-2): flight-free zones, minimum altitudes, VFR transit corridors at set altitudes. Use the Grand Canyon VFR Aeronautical Chart.

sections.intro: Dave goes through the sectional symbol by symbol. Know everything in the airport data block and the VOR box.
qs: Sectional review: roads, railroads, airspace, frequencies, UNICOM, pilot-controlled lighting, part-time tower, max elevation figures/obstruction heights.
Know the legend: CTAF/UNICOM, ★L (part-time lighting), PCL frequency and clicks, “C” in a circle = CTAF, tower hours in the Chart Supplement, MEFs, obstruction heights (MSL vs AGL).
Airport data block: field elevation, runway length, *L, CTAF, tower frequency, right/left pattern, star next to tower frequency.

Elevation is first in the line; runway length is the longest runway in hundreds of feet; L = lighting sunset to sunrise, *L = lighting limitations (check the Chart Supplement); © = CTAF; CT = tower frequency, ★ = part-time tower; RP = right pattern.
Where do you find runway surface information? How do you know fuel is available?
Chart Supplement for surface. Fuel/services: tick marks around the airport symbol on the sectional (details in the Chart Supplement).
Rotating beacon: what’s the symbol and what do the colors mean?

Star above the airport symbol. White-green = lighted civil land airport; white-yellow = water; white-white-green = military. Beacon on during the day in Class B, C, D or E surface area may mean below VFR minimums.
VOR box: FSS name, FSS frequency, nav frequency, underline, the R (e.g. 122.1R).
Underlined frequency = no voice on that frequency. 122.1R = FSS receives only on 122.1: transmit on 122.1, listen on the VOR frequency. Heavy-line box = FSS co-located.
VORTAC = VOR + TACAN (military nav; civil aircraft get DME from it). VOR-DME = VOR with civil DME.
Obstruction and group obstruction symbols? What altitude are they at?
Single vs group obstruction symbols; bold number = top in MSL, number in parentheses = height AGL; taller symbol for 1,000 ft AGL or more; flash marks = lighted.
Roads, railroads, highways, rivers, lakes: what do they look like?
Know the legend symbols and use them as checkpoints.
Identify Class A, B, C, D, E and G on the sectional with their floors and ceilings.
Solid blue = B; solid magenta = C; dashed blue = D; dashed magenta = E to the surface; magenta shading = E at 700 AGL; blue shading = E at 1,200 AGL. A starts at 18,000 MSL.
What is a Class E extension?
Class E surface extension (dashed magenta) beyond the Class C/D surface area for instrument approaches; no tower contact needed.
Terminal radar service area: gray outline; participation is voluntary.
Where do you find frequencies and the controlling agency for a restricted area?
Special use airspace table on the margin/back of the sectional.

Hot spot 1: a spot on the airport with a history or risk of collisions or runway incursions where extra attention is needed. Shown on airport diagrams and in the Chart Supplement. Mike: it’s fine if it takes a second; he cares that you know what it means for safe taxi.
The “rocket ship” game: pick a point on the sectional and climb straight up. What airspace are you in at each altitude?
Name every class and its floor and ceiling on the way up (e.g. G → E at 700/1,200 AGL → B or C shelves → E → A at 18,000 MSL).

sections.intro: From the Blitz PPL mock oral.
qs: What is an approach lighting system (ALS)?
Lights extending out from the runway threshold to help transition from instruments to visual.
VASI and PAPI: how do you read them?
VASI: red over white on glidepath (“red over white, you’re all right”). PAPI: 2 white and 2 red on glidepath.
Runway end identifier lights: a pair of synchronized flashing lights at the threshold.
What colors are runway and taxiway lights?
Runway edges white (yellow in the last 2,000 ft on instrument runways), threshold green, runway end red. Taxiway edges blue, centerlines green.
Key the mic on the CTAF/PCL frequency: 7 times in 5 sec high, 5 medium, 3 low.
What does the rotating beacon tell you?
White-green: lighted civil land airport. White-yellow: water. Dual white-green: military. On during the day in controlled airspace may mean below VFR minimums.
What does it mean if the rotating beacon is on during the day? night?

At night a rotating beacon helps identify the airport. In Class B/C/D/E surface areas, daytime beacon operation often indicates ceiling below 1,000 feet and/or visibility below three SM, but its operation is not a reliable weather determination. Obtain actual observations and comply with weather rules regardless of whether the beacon is on.
What does an X on a runway mean?

An X indicates a closed runway or portion of one. A temporary closure may use a lighted or otherwise temporary X. Verify NOTAMs and airport information; do not assume a runway is usable just because its surface appears clear or its numbers remain visible.
There are two large numbers near the end of the runway. What do they mean?

Runway numbers represent approximately the magnetic approach direction rounded to the nearest ten degrees with the last digit removed. Runway 18 points approximately 180 degrees magnetic; its opposite is normally 36. Parallel runways add L, C, or R. The marking is an identifier, not a precision compass reference.
Describe the procedure for using each of the three VFR routes through the Los Angeles Class B airspace.

This is a local question from an old worksheet; do not memorize its claim that there are only three routes. Use the current Los Angeles TAC, published transition/SFRA procedures, NOTAMs, and ATC availability. Coastal, Hollywood Park, Coliseum, Mini Route, and SFRA are names encountered in FAA material, but authorization and availability must be verified. A Class B transition needs an explicit clearance unless an applicable published exception, such as compliant SFRA operation, applies.

An Alert Area identifies a high volume of pilot training or unusual aerial activity. It is charted with an A-number. Entry is not generally prohibited, but all pilots remain responsible for collision avoidance. Read the charted activity, altitudes, times, and controlling information.
What is a Military Training Route? Find one on the sectional.

Military Training Routes support high-speed low-altitude military training. IR denotes an IFR route and VR a VFR route. Four-digit route numbers have no segment above 1,500 AGL; three-digit numbers include at least one segment above 1,500 AGL. Check current route activity with Flight Service when relevant and maintain a strong traffic scan.
What is the emergency frequency? When/how do you use it?

121.5 MHz is the civil VHF emergency frequency. Use it when you need urgent assistance and cannot obtain it on your current ATC frequency. State MAYDAY for distress, identify yourself, describe the problem, position, altitude, fuel/time, persons aboard, and intentions as practical. If already communicating with ATC, your current frequency often provides the fastest help.
What frequency is set aside for pilots to use for air to air communications?

122.75 MHz is the standard frequency for private fixed-wing air-to-air communications; 123.025 is used for helicopter air-to-air. Use the proper frequency for the operation and location. 123.45 is not the general domestic casual air-to-air frequency, and an air-to-air frequency does not replace CTAF or required ATC communications.
You are about to enter the Class C airspace. What information should you give on the initial call?

State the facility name, your callsign, aircraft type, position, altitude, and request, with the ATIS code when relevant. Example: Approach, Cessna 123AB, ten miles west, four thousand five hundred, inbound full stop with Bravo. Establish two-way communication before entry; a response using your callsign generally establishes it unless ATC directs you to remain outside.
You are in the Class C airspace. The controller issues you a heading and altitude which will take you through a small cloud? What should you do?

Tell ATC immediately: Unable, VFR; request a heading or altitude that maintains VFR. Do not enter the cloud merely because a controller issued instructions. If already unable to maintain VFR, explain the situation and request immediate assistance; declare an emergency if necessary. Controllers do not take over your responsibility to maintain VFR.
Describe the airport traffic pattern; which direction turns are standard; how to determine whether this airport/runway uses standard or non-standard pattern. (Gouge: without the sectional?)

A standard pattern uses left turns and includes upwind, crosswind, downwind, base, and final. A 45-degree entry to midfield downwind is commonly recommended at non-towered airports. Verify right traffic through chart RP notes, the Chart Supplement, traffic indicators, and published procedures. Account for actual traffic, wind, terrain, and tower instructions. Gouge: Segmented circle / traffic pattern indicators, the Chart Supplement, ask UNICOM. Default is left traffic unless marked otherwise. Steve: pattern entry procedures.
Describe the procedure for getting clearance into the Class D airspace.

Class D generally requires two-way radio communication with the controlling tower before entry, rather than an explicit Class B-style entry clearance. A reply using your callsign normally establishes communication; Aircraft calling, standby does not. Remain outside if instructed. Landing still requires a landing clearance, and special authorizations may be necessary after radio failure.
How do you know the traffic pattern altitude at an unfamiliar airport? Runway lengths/widths?

Location of hazards? Availability of services? ATlS, tower and ground frequencies? FSS telephone numbers? Use the current Chart Supplement, sectional/TAC, airport diagram, NOTAMs, and reliable airport information. These provide traffic pattern altitude, runway dimensions, hazards, services, hours, lighting, and frequencies. Check airport remarks and temporary changes rather than relying solely on a map's runway graphic or an old saved frequency.
Describe airspeeds, altitudes, gear, flap and power settings to be used on the 45, downwind, base and final.

Aircraft-specific: use the POH/AFM, school procedures, current weight, wind, and runway situation. Arrive stabilized at the published traffic-pattern altitude, configure within limits, and use the recommended approach speeds. Do not invent universal Cessna/Piper speeds or power settings. Brief target speeds and configurations for your actual airplane before the flight.
Describe the procedure for a short field landing. A soft field landing. A short field takeoff, and a soft field takeoff.

Short-field landing: use approved configuration and speed, a precise aiming point, minimal float, and approved braking. Soft-field landing: maintain control while touching gently and keeping weight off the nosewheel. Short-field takeoff: use approved flap/power procedures and obstacle speed. Soft-field takeoff: keep moving where appropriate, unload the nosewheel, lift off smoothly, and accelerate in ground effect before climbing. Follow the aircraft checklist.
Compare the communications requirements at tower vs. non-tower airports.

At towered airports, establish required communications and obtain the necessary taxi, runway-crossing, takeoff, and landing clearances. At most non-towered airports, self-announce on CTAF and fit safely into traffic; radio use is generally recommended rather than universally required for all aircraft. Separate airspace rules may still require communications or equipment.

An intersection takeoff starts from a taxiway intersection instead of the full runway end. It reduces available takeoff distance. Determine the actual usable distance, calculate performance with a margin, and decline if unsuitable. A clearance to depart from an intersection is not an assurance that your airplane can safely do so.

A NOTAM is a time-sensitive notice concerning facilities, services, procedures, or hazards essential to flight operations. Examples include runway closures, navigation outages, changed lighting, and certain airspace restrictions. Read the effective times, altitude limits, location, and text; a graphical symbol alone can omit essential details.
What is a position report? Is it required VFR?
Your position, time, altitude and next fix. Not required VFR; helpful for search and rescue and traffic.
How do you give a position report?
Identification, position, time, altitude, type of flight plan, ETA and name of next reporting point.
How do you change a flight plan in flight?

For a VFR flight plan, contact Flight Service to amend route, destination, or estimated arrival time and ensure the change is understood. For ATC clearances, request the amendment from ATC. Editing a route in an EFB does not automatically amend an activated plan or ATC clearance. Close the VFR plan after arrival.
What is an airway? Find one on the sectional chart.

An airway is a published route through designated airspace, commonly used for IFR navigation. Low-altitude VOR Federal airways are identified with V-numbers and shown on appropriate charts, including many sectionals. Their depiction does not automatically impose a VFR clearance requirement or establish terrain clearance for every VFR altitude you might choose.

When weather permits, each pilot must maintain vigilance to see and avoid other aircraft, whether operating VFR or IFR. Scan systematically, account for blind spots, clear before maneuvering, and use lights and traffic information appropriately. ADS-B traffic, flight following, and right-of-way rules supplement visual collision avoidance; none guarantees separation from every aircraft.
What is an ADIZ? Why do you care?

An ADIZ is an Air Defense Identification Zone. Crossing or operating within one can require a defense flight plan, position reports, communication, and transponder procedures under Part 99. International entry has additional requirements. Review the current ADIZ procedures for the actual route; it is not simply another Class B/C/D airspace category.
What actions can you take to get help in an emergency?

Fly the airplane, identify a safe course of action, run the appropriate checklist, and communicate early. Use your current ATC frequency or 121.5, declare an emergency when warranted, and squawk 7700 when appropriate. Request vectors, airport information, weather, emergency equipment, or other help. Activate an ELT or personal locator device as appropriate after a forced landing.
The following are codes for use in your transponder. When would you use each? 1200, 7500, 7600, 7700

1200: ordinary VFR operation in the U.S. when not assigned another code. 7500: unlawful interference/hijacking. 7600: radio communication failure. 7700: emergency. If already receiving ATC services, retain the assigned code unless instructed otherwise or circumstances warrant changing it; tell ATC the emergency promptly when able.
When a part-time tower closes, what airspace does it become?

Usually Class E surface area (if weather reporting is available) or Class G. Check the Chart Supplement for that airport. Mike: Ogden’s Class D when the tower closes → Class E. Where’s that found? Chart Supplement / airport diagram legend.

sections.intro: From the Blitz PPL mock oral. Steve is big on icing and gives METAR/TAF go/no-go scenarios; he called it an automatic fail not to use the POH for true airspeed.
qs: The National Weather Service is part of NOAA and provides weather observations, forecasts, and warnings. Its Aviation Weather Center produces aviation-focused products. Pilots use those products with other reliable information to evaluate conditions for the entire route and flight period.
How do you get a preflight weather briefing?

Use Flight Service by telephone or online, Aviation Weather Center products, and a suitable EFB briefing service. Review observations, forecasts, advisories, radar/satellite, winds, NOTAMs, and restrictions. Record the briefing and obtain updates near departure. A weather app showing one airport's conditions is not a complete preflight evaluation. Gouge: Standard briefing from an approved source: adverse conditions, METARs, TAFs, GFA, winds aloft, PIREPs, NOTAMs, TFRs.
What is an area forecast? Winds aloft forecast?

An area forecast describes broad regional weather. The legacy CONUS text FA was replaced by graphical products, including the Graphical Forecasts for Aviation. Winds/temperatures aloft forecasts describe expected conditions at specified levels and times. Check product coverage, validity, and units; not every historical forecast product remains available in every region.
What is a TAF? What is a METAR?

A METAR is an airport surface weather observation; SPECI is a special observation issued for significant changes. A TAF is a terminal aerodrome forecast describing expected conditions near an airport during its stated validity period. A TAF is not an en route forecast, and a METAR describes observed conditions rather than guaranteeing future weather. Gouge: METAR: observation, hourly (SPECI when conditions change significantly). TAF: forecast for 5 sm around the airport, issued 4 times a day (00, 06, 12, 18Z), valid 24 or 30 hr. Mike: just read and interpret them.
Winds aloft forecasts give wind in true or magnetic bearing?

Forecast winds aloft are referenced to true north. Convert appropriately when calculating a magnetic heading. Do not assume all aviation wind sources use the same reference: runway-facing tower/ATIS wind information is normally magnetic, while coded weather products such as METARs use true direction.
Wind speeds are in knots or miles per hour?

Aviation wind speeds in standard U.S. METARs and winds-aloft products are normally knots, shown by the product's units or code. One knot equals one nautical mile per hour. Verify units on unfamiliar products, especially general weather apps that may display miles per hour or meters per second.
What is ATlS? How do you get it?

ATIS is Automatic Terminal Information Service, a repeating airport weather and operational broadcast, often available by radio and sometimes digitally. Obtain it before contacting the facility when practical and report its identifying letter. Listen to the complete message for runway, approach, closure, and operational information as well as weather. Gouge: AWOS/ASOS: automated weather observations, often at non-towered fields. ATIS: recorded broadcast at towered airports with weather, runways in use, NOTAMs and other info, updated hourly or as changes occur.
The recording says ~. ..temperature 54, dewpoint 52... What does this mean to you?

The temperature-dewpoint spread is small, indicating moist air near saturation and possible fog or low-cloud development if conditions support it. It does not guarantee fog. The old worksheet uses values that may imply Fahrenheit; modern U.S. aviation reports normally give temperature/dewpoint in Celsius, so confirm the units and reporting source.
Why do they broadcast the altimeter setting?

The local altimeter setting lets you adjust the altimeter so it indicates approximately the airport elevation on the ground and supports consistent indicated altitude nearby. Pressure changes can create substantial errors. Flying from higher pressure toward lower pressure without updating the setting causes true altitude to be lower than indicated.
Wind shear: what is it and what do you do?
Sudden change in wind speed/direction over a short distance; abrupt airspeed and flight path changes. Avoid known LLWS; delay or go around.
Airframe icing: what does it do?
Changes airfoil shape, increases drag and weight, raises stall speed. Avoid it in an unapproved airplane; exit promptly.
Carburetor icing: what is it and how do you fix it?
Cooling in the carb venturi freezes moisture and blocks airflow. Carb heat per the POH.
Ice blocking the air intake/induction system; fuel-injected engines can get it too. Use alternate air.
Clear air turbulence: what is it?
Turbulence with no cloud cues, often near jet streams, wind shear or mountain waves. Check forecasts and PIREPs.
Strong vertical currents, turbulence, lightning, hail, wind shear, thunderstorms. Avoid by a wide margin.
Towering cumulus: what does it tell you?
Rapid vertical growth, unstable air, possibly developing thunderstorms. Avoid them.
Microbursts: what are they and what happens if you fly through one?
Intense small downdraft. Headwind and airspeed gain, then strong sink, then tailwind and airspeed loss. Very dangerous near the ground.
Hail: where and why is it dangerous?
Damages the airframe, windshield and engine; can fall outside the storm or under the anvil. Avoid the storm.
Temperature inversion: what is it and what does it cause?
Temperature increases with height. Traps haze and pollution, can cause fog and low-level wind shear.
Cool, moist air near the coast under an inversion: low stratus and fog.
Wake turbulence: how do you avoid it?
Stay above the larger aircraft’s flight path and land beyond its touchdown point; take off before its rotation point. Strongest behind heavy, clean, slow aircraft.
Moist air moving over a colder surface cools to saturation; wind can sustain it over large coastal areas.
The best course of action to take if you accidentally fly into a cloud is?

Maintain aircraft control using the instruments, keep a safe airspeed, and avoid abrupt maneuvering. Engage a suitable autopilot only if trained and it is functioning properly. Contact ATC immediately, declare an emergency when warranted, and obtain help reaching VMC while considering terrain. A controlled return toward known VMC may be appropriate; an automatic steep turn is not.
Describe the hazards of wingtip vortices, the conditions under which you might expect to encounter them, and how to avoid them.

Wake vortices are strongest behind aircraft that are heavy, clean, and slow. They generally descend and drift with wind. Avoid the preceding aircraft's flightpath: on landing stay above its path and touch down beyond its touchdown point; on takeoff plan to rotate before its rotation point and remain above its path when appropriate. If separation or geometry is doubtful, wait or go around. Mike (11/17): how should you land behind a bigger jet? Stay above its glidepath and land beyond its touchdown point.
The average life span of a VFR pilot in the clouds is?

There is no valid universal average survival time for every VFR pilot who enters clouds. The often-repeated 178-second figure comes from a limited historical demonstration and should not be taught as a personal countdown. The useful lesson is that spatial disorientation and loss of control can occur quickly; maintain instrument control and request immediate help.

A graveyard spiral is an unnoticed descending turn that may develop after vestibular sensations fade. Pulling back to stop the descent can tighten the turn and increase load factor. Recognize it using instruments and recover with the trained unusual-attitude procedure while controlling power, airspeed, and bank; do not rely on bodily sensations.

Flicker vertigo is discomfort or disorientation caused by flashing light, such as sunlight interrupted by a propeller or strobe reflections. Symptoms can include nausea and impaired concentration. Reduce exposure with a sun visor, appropriate lighting changes, or a heading change when safe, and transfer control if needed.
What are the early symptoms of hypoxia?
Euphoria, headache, impaired judgment, drowsiness, tingling, cyanosis.
Hypoxic vs hypemic hypoxia? Other types?
Hypoxic: not enough O2 available (altitude). Hypemic: blood can’t carry O2 (CO, anemia, blood donation). Also stagnant and histotoxic.
What true airspeed did you use for your cross-country and where did it come from?
From the POH cruise performance chart for your altitude, temperature and power setting. Never guess: TAS drives groundspeed, time and fuel.
Why did you choose your cruise altitude? What factors?

Winds aloft, terrain and obstacles, airspace, VFR cruising altitudes by magnetic course (91.159: odd +500 east, even +500 west above 3,000 AGL), cloud clearance, performance, gliding distance, oxygen.
What does structural ice do aerodynamically?

Disrupts airflow over the wing: less lift, more drag, more weight, higher stall speed, stall at a lower AOA; tail ice can cause tailplane stall. Also blocks pitot/static and antennas. Steve: define wind shear; what signs do you look for to avoid icing. He wants good ADM: you’d go land.
What do you do if you encounter icing?
Exit the conditions (turn around, change altitude toward warmer air), pitot heat and carb heat on, increase power, avoid flap changes, tell ATC, land with extra speed.
Here’s a METAR and TAF. Would you go?
Decode it and make a real go/no-go call against VFR mins and personal minimums. Expect several versions.
Atmospheric factors affecting takeoffs and landings?
Wind (headwind, crosswind, gusts, wind shear), density altitude, thermals and turbulence from uneven surface heating.
Weather associated with thunderstorms? How far away do you stay?
Turbulence, hail, icing, lightning, wind shear, microbursts, heavy rain, low ceilings. Stay at least 20 nm from severe storms.
What’s a microburst? What happens if you fly through one?

An intense, small downdraft (usually under about 2.5 mi across, lasting ~15 min). Entering: headwind and airspeed gain; middle: strong downdraft; exiting: tailwind and big airspeed loss with sink. Very dangerous near the ground on takeoff or landing.
Carbon monoxide poisoning: symptoms and fix?
Headache, drowsiness, dizziness, nausea. Cabin heat off, fresh air vents open, oxygen if available, land. CO detector helps catch it.
Visual: autokinesis, false horizon, black-hole approach, featureless terrain, flicker vertigo. Vestibular: leans, Coriolis, graveyard spiral, somatogravic, inversion, elevator. Trust the instruments.
True airspeed vs groundspeed: what’s the difference, and how do headwinds change them?
TAS is speed through the air (from the POH for your altitude/temp/power); groundspeed is speed over the ground. A headwind lowers groundspeed but not TAS, so time and fuel go up.
Your own ceiling, visibility, wind/crosswind and other limits, set above the legal minimums based on experience. Have them written down. Mike: he liked a booklet with personal minimums written down.
Walk through your ForeFlight briefing: what does each diagram tell you?
Fronts, high and low pressure, clouds with and without vertical development, lapse rate, atmospheric temperature and pressure.

Stable vs unstable air, standard lapse rate ~2°C/1,000 ft, moisture + lift + instability for vertical development. Mike (11/17): noticeable differences with a cold front: the answer he wanted was simply “colder” (also wind shift, pressure rise, gusty, showers, then clearing).

sections.intro: From the Blitz PPL mock oral. Dave asked what causes lift and emphasized wingtip vortices in ground effect.
qs: VSO: stall speed in landing configuration (bottom of the white arc). VS1: stall speed in a specified configuration, usually clean (bottom of the green arc).
What are VR, VX and VY?
VR: rotation. VX: best angle of climb (most altitude per distance). VY: best rate of climb (most altitude per time).
What is VA, and how does weight change it?
Design maneuvering speed: full, abrupt control deflection won’t overstress the airplane. Decreases as weight decreases.
VNO: max structural cruising speed (top of the green arc; above it smooth air only). VNE: never exceed (red line).
What are VFE, VLO and VLE?
VFE: max flap-extended speed (top of the white arc). VLO: max gear operating speed. VLE: max gear extended speed.
The POH speed for maximum glide distance at max weight (lower at lighter weights).
What are g-forces? How are they created? How much can your aircraft take?

G-force describes acceleration/load relative to normal gravity. Aerodynamic maneuvering and gusts change load factor, the ratio of lift to weight. Obtain the actual positive/negative limits and flap-related limits from the POH, placards, and category limitations. Published structural limits are not permission for aggressive maneuvering, and maneuvering speed does not protect against every control input.
What is the relationship between angle of bank, g force, and stall speed?

In a coordinated level turn, load factor equals 1/cos(bank angle). At 60 degrees bank it is 2 G, so stall speed is approximately 1.414 times the 1-G value for the same configuration and weight. Bank alone does not always determine load factor; the relationship assumes altitude is maintained in a coordinated turn.

An accelerated stall occurs when the critical angle of attack is exceeded at a load factor above 1 G, so it can happen at a higher airspeed than the familiar wings-level stall speed. Prevent it through smooth loading and angle-of-attack awareness. Recovery requires reducing angle of attack, followed by the appropriate aircraft procedure.

Cross-controlled usually means opposing aileron and rudder inputs. It may be intentional in a slip, but excessive rudder with opposite aileron in a skidding base-to-final turn is particularly dangerous near the stall. Recognize whether the airplane is slipping or skidding, manage angle of attack, and avoid trying to force a turn with rudder.

In a slip, the airplane moves sideways toward the inside of the turn; in a skid, it moves toward the outside. In a conventional turn, the slip/skid ball is toward the inside during a slip and outside during a skid. A deliberate forward slip can steepen descent, and a sideslip can correct crosswind drift when approved.

Adverse yaw is yaw opposite the intended roll, largely associated with the drag difference between the wings as ailerons change lift. Apply coordinated rudder as needed rather than using a fixed amount. It is often more noticeable at low airspeed with larger control deflections.
Discuss torque, slipstream effect, and p-factor.

For the typical clockwise-turning propeller viewed from the cockpit: torque tends to roll the airplane left; spiraling slipstream strikes the left side of the vertical tail and tends to yaw left; P-factor produces asymmetric thrust at a positive propeller-disc angle of attack, tending to yaw left. Their relative strength varies with power, speed, and attitude.
Discuss stalls and spins (definition, prevention, recognition and recovery)

A stall occurs when the wing exceeds critical angle of attack, at any airspeed or attitude. A spin involves stalled flight with autorotation and yaw. Prevent spins through coordination and stall avoidance. Recover stalls by reducing angle of attack and following the POH; recover a spin only with the aircraft's approved procedure. Never assume a generic mnemonic overrides the POH or that intentional spins are approved. Mike: spends a lot of time on stalls: how dangerous they are and the correct wording for recovery (reduce the angle of attack). Spins: PARE recovery, why you push forward at the end (break the stall once rotation stops), and the base-to-final skidding turn stall/spin danger. Mike: PARE: power idle, ailerons neutral, rudder opposite, elevator forward; neutralize when rotation stops, recover from the dive. Also how CG affects stall likelihood. Mike (11/17): he leads with the nose-down stall / relative wind discussion (see the next question).
Does attitude control a stall? Can you stall with the nose down?

No. A stall happens at the critical angle of attack, which depends on the relative wind, not the pitch attitude. You can stall nose-down (e.g. pulling hard out of a dive or a steep descending turn). Recovery is always reduce the AOA relative to the relative wind. This took about a quarter of the 11/17 oral: answering “yes, attitude controls stalls” is the trap.
What is Zulu time? Greenwich Mean Time?

Zulu means UTC, the worldwide aviation time reference. GMT is a historical term often used informally for the same practical clock reference. Utah is UTC minus seven hours during Mountain Standard Time and minus six during Mountain Daylight Time. Convert carefully across midnight because the UTC date may differ.

An airfoil's shape and angle of attack influence airflow, pressure distribution, and aerodynamic forces. Lift acts perpendicular to relative wind; drag acts parallel and opposite to relative wind. Pressure differences and downward airflow deflection are consistent explanations of lift. Increasing angle of attack increases lift only until the critical region and stall behavior are reached. Gouge: Pressure difference over and under the wing (Bernoulli) plus air deflected downward (Newton’s 3rd law), from AOA and airfoil shape.
Compare parasite drag and induced drag

Parasite drag includes form, interference, and skin-friction drag and generally increases with airspeed. Induced drag is associated with lift production and generally increases at low speed for a given required lift. Their combined curve explains why both very slow and very fast flight can require more thrust than flight near minimum drag.
Discuss density altitude What 3 parts of the airplane does it affect?

Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature. High elevation, high temperature, and humidity reduce air density and performance. Expect longer takeoff distance and reduced climb, with reduced power in normally aspirated engines. Compute performance using the POH and actual conditions; the same indicated airspeed corresponds to higher true airspeed at higher density altitude. Gouge: Pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature. Thinner air hurts the engine (less power), the propeller (less thrust) and the wings (less lift): longer takeoff roll, lower climb rate.
Discuss leaning procedures for your aircraft.

Aircraft-specific: follow the engine and airframe manufacturer's procedures for the installed fuel system and instruments. Leaning may be appropriate for taxi, cruise, and high-density-altitude takeoff, but mixture targets and restrictions differ. Do not apply a universal EGT target or always-full-rich rule. Brief the actual takeoff, climb, cruise, and descent procedures from the POH.
Discuss detonation and pre-ignition: definitions, causes, effects, relationship, and prevention.

Detonation is abnormal explosive combustion of the remaining fuel-air charge after normal ignition. Preignition is ignition before the intended spark, often from a hot spot. Both can produce destructive temperatures and pressure. Use approved fuel, correct mixture/power, and adequate cooling. They can contribute to each other; reduce power and follow the POH if abnormal engine indications develop.
Discuss stall characteristics of clean vs. flaps down.

Flaps generally increase maximum lift and reduce stall speed, while changing drag, pitch, and the stall attitude. A clean airplane usually stalls at a higher indicated speed for the same weight/load factor. Exact warning, break, wing-drop behavior, and recovery requirements are aircraft-specific. Both configurations stall because critical angle of attack is exceeded.

Gyroscopic precession means a force applied to a rotating propeller disc produces a response approximately 90 degrees later in the direction of rotation. In a conventional clockwise-propeller tailwheel airplane, raising the tail can produce a left-yawing tendency. The direction depends on the imposed pitch change and rotation; it is not always a left force in every maneuver.
Do a weight and balance for today’s flight. Discuss results.

A valid calculation requires your airplane's current empty weight/moment, occupants, baggage, usable fuel, station arms, and expected fuel burn. Add weights and moments, divide total moment by total weight for CG, and check takeoff and landing conditions against all limits. No aircraft/loading data were supplied, so a numerical result cannot be honestly calculated. Gouge: Compute from the POH; within limits for takeoff and landing; know what happens forward vs aft CG. ForeFlight: it uses the aircraft profile’s empty weight/moment and station arms, so verify the profile matches the airplane’s actual W&B record.
What would you expect of an aircraft loaded beyond its CG limits?

A forward CG generally increases stability and control forces and may reduce flare/elevator authority while increasing stall speed. An aft CG reduces longitudinal stability and can seriously impair stall/spin recovery. An airplane can be below maximum gross weight and still be outside its CG envelope. Correct loading before flight. Mike: covers the CG characteristics of your airplane and how CG changes as weight changes. Mike: forward vs aft CG.
Scenario: high density altitude day. Would you take off?

Work it out in the POH. Gouge: runway length was enough to lift off, but not to clear the 50 ft obstacle at that density altitude → don’t go. Steve: gouge 2: 50 ft obstacle at the end of a 4,200 ft runway at max takeoff weight. Use POH charts and pressure vs density altitude. Answer: no.
What is ground effect and what causes it?
Within about one wingspan of the ground, the surface reduces wingtip vortices, upwash and downwash. Less induced drag, airplane floats or lifts off early. Dave emphasized wingtip vortices.
Maneuvering speed (Va): what is it and how does weight change it?
Max speed for full, abrupt control deflection without overstressing the airplane: below Va it stalls first. Va decreases as weight decreases.
What will your takeoff ground roll be today? How does it change with higher altitude, higher temperature, and runway slope?

Work it out from the POH takeoff chart (pressure altitude, temperature, weight, wind, surface). Higher altitude and temperature = longer roll; upslope = longer, downslope = shorter. Mike (11/17): gouge: 7°C at KOGD; rounded up to 10°C and 5,000 ft to be conservative. Factors that increase takeoff roll; a grass runway correction is in the notes under the POH chart.

sections.intro: From the Blitz PPL mock oral. Many answers are aircraft-specific: use the POH for the checkride airplane.
qs: Alternator or generator? What’s the difference?
Most trainers have an alternator: it produces power even at low RPM, generators don’t. Check your airplane.
Is it belt or gear driven, and what’s its capacity?
Aircraft-specific: check POH Sec 7 (e.g. amps and voltage).
Is there an avionics master switch in the aircraft? Where?

Aircraft-specific: locate the actual avionics master or individual avionics power controls and know which buses they switch. Some aircraft have split buses, essential buses, or no traditional avionics master. Follow the startup/shutdown checklist; never assume switching it off removes power from every electronic device.
Where are the alternator field and bus circuit breakers/fuses?

Aircraft-specific: identify the marked alternator field, alternator output/bus protection, and essential-bus protections in the actual panel and schematic. Know what each protects. Do not repeatedly reset a tripped breaker or replace a fuse with a larger one; follow the POH and maintenance guidance because an electrical fault can create a fire.
Does this aircraft have an over voltage protection circuit? Describe its operation including any potential “false activations.”

Aircraft-specific: many systems sense excessive voltage and disconnect alternator excitation/output to protect equipment. The warning indications and approved reset procedures vary. A transient may trigger a protective trip, but do not dismiss an indication as false without following the checklist and confirming normal operation. Repeated resetting can mask a dangerous fault. Mike: overvoltage scenario: explain how to solve it.
Describe the use of the EGT and CHT gauges, if so equipped.

EGT measures exhaust gas temperature and can support mixture adjustment and cylinder comparisons using the approved procedure. CHT measures cylinder head temperature and helps monitor thermal stress and cooling. Neither replaces the other. Interpret trends alongside oil temperature/pressure, power, and engine smoothness; operating limits and targets come from the engine/airframe manuals.
Describe the vacuum system. Which gyros are vacuum driven, and which are electric?

Aircraft-specific: traditional panels may use an engine-driven vacuum pump for attitude and heading gyros, while the turn coordinator is often electric. Modern electronic displays may use electric sensors and have backup batteries. Identify your actual power sources, suction indication, failure cues, and backup instruments; a familiar-looking panel does not guarantee a familiar system.
How does the pitot-static system work?

The airspeed indicator compares pitot pressure with static pressure; the altimeter and VSI use static pressure. If pitot inlet and drain both block, the airspeed indicator can behave like an altimeter. A static blockage freezes the altimeter, drives VSI toward zero, and causes airspeed errors during altitude changes. Use approved pitot heat/alternate-static procedures and applicable corrections.
What is the rate of climb at 8000 feet pressure altitude, 90 degrees F?

A numerical climb rate cannot be supplied without the specific POH chart, aircraft weight, configuration, power, and other chart assumptions. Convert 90 F to about 32 C, enter at 8,000 feet pressure altitude, interpolate only as permitted, and apply chart notes. If outside chart limits, do not extrapolate a reassuring number. Account for terrain and downdrafts as well as still-air climb.
What is the difference between a SIGMET and an AIRMET? CONVECTIVE SIGMET?

AIRMETs/G-AIRMETs advise of specified widespread hazards such as IFR/mountain obscuration, turbulence, or icing, with format depending on region. SIGMETs address significant nonconvective hazards such as severe turbulence, severe icing, or volcanic ash. Convective SIGMETs address qualifying thunderstorm hazards. Read the actual phenomenon, area, altitude, and validity; any can be consequential to a light airplane. Gouge: AIRMET S (IFR, mountain obscuration), T (moderate turbulence, sfc wind >30 kt, LLWS), Z (moderate icing, freezing level). SIGMET: severe icing, severe/extreme turbulence, dust/sandstorms, volcanic ash. Convective SIGMET: thunderstorms (lines, embedded, severe), hail ≥¾ in, tornadoes.
Ceilings are in feet; is this MSL or AGL?

METAR/TAF cloud-base heights and reported ceilings are generally AGL at the reporting airport. A ceiling is the lowest broken or overcast layer or vertical visibility into obscuration. Other products may use MSL, flight levels, or explicitly labeled AGL values. Always check the product legend rather than applying the airport-report convention to every chart.
Discuss the ceilings, visibility, cloud types and turbulence, which are to be expected in stable vs. unstable air.

Stable air often supports smooth air, stratiform clouds, steady precipitation, and poorer visibility, especially under inversions. Unstable air supports vertical motion, cumuliform clouds, showery precipitation, turbulence, and sometimes thunderstorms; visibility may be better outside precipitation. Moisture, lift, and local conditions determine whether clouds actually form and how low their bases are.
Under what weather conditions is carburetor icing most likely?

Carburetor ice can form with substantial moisture even when outside air temperature is well above freezing, because pressure drop and fuel vaporization cool the carburetor. Reduced power can increase susceptibility. On a fixed-pitch propeller airplane, an unexplained RPM decrease may be a cue. Apply carburetor heat according to the POH; initial roughness or power loss can occur while ice melts. Steve: what does a carburetor do, what’s the downside (carb ice), and what conditions cause it?
How is an aircraft ignition system different than a car? Will the engine run on the magnetos alone?

Many training-airplane piston engines use two engine-driven magnetos and two spark plugs per cylinder. Magnetos supply ignition independently of the aircraft battery/alternator, unlike most automotive systems. Some aircraft use electronic ignition with different power dependencies. Explain the installed system rather than assuming every aircraft engine can run without electrical power. Gouge: Self-contained, engine-driven generators that make spark independent of the electrical system; the engine keeps running with the master off. Two for redundancy and better combustion.
What is the magneto ground wire? Why is it important?

The magneto P-lead grounds the magneto primary circuit to stop its spark production. Selecting OFF should ground both magnetos. A broken lead can leave a magneto live even with the key off, making propeller movement dangerous. Treat every propeller as capable of starting the engine and follow approved shutdown/check procedures.
Compare/contrast dead reckoning, pilotage and radio navigation.

Pilotage uses visible landmarks. Dead reckoning estimates position using heading/course, groundspeed, and elapsed time with wind corrections. Radio navigation uses signals from systems such as VOR/DME or satellite navigation. Cross-check independent methods so one incorrect waypoint, wind estimate, or receiver indication does not go unnoticed.
Is the fuel pump required to be on or off for takeoff and landing?

Aircraft-specific: use the POH. Many low-wing airplanes require an electric boost pump for takeoff and landing; some high-wing gravity-fed systems do not have that requirement or equipment. Pump operation, fuel pressure checks, and emergency uses differ. Do not transfer a Piper fuel-pump habit to another aircraft without checking.
Is your engine fuel injected or carbureted? What difference does this make?

The source text is corrupted; this question concerns fuel injection versus carburetion. A carburetor mixes fuel/air before induction distribution and may require carburetor heat. Fuel injection meters fuel to individual intake areas and does not have carburetor icing, but can still have intake/induction icing and different starting issues. Identify your actual system and its approved procedures. V-speed definitions are in Question 95.
Describe the fuel system: tanks, valves, drains, cross feeds, vents, return lines, gasolator, required fuel grades, system capacity.

Aircraft-specific: trace fuel from each tank through selectors, vents, strainers, pumps, and metering equipment to the engine. Identify drains, usable/unusable capacity, approved grade, selector restrictions, and return lines if installed. Many single-engine trainers have no crossfeed system. Confirm fuel quantity visually using an approved method, sample all required drains, and explain what happens if a vent blocks. Gouge: Tanks → selector → strainer/gascolator → (electric/engine-driven pump on low wing, gravity on high wing) → carburetor or fuel injection → cylinders. Vents and sumps. Steve: electrical system and the gravity-fed fuel system rundown.
Which direction does the CG move as fuel is burned?

It depends on the tanks' location relative to the aircraft's current CG. Removing fuel shifts CG away from the fuel station: fuel aft of CG generally moves CG forward as it burns, and fuel forward of CG generally moves it aft. Calculate using the actual loading data rather than assuming one direction for all airplanes.

Same topic as Question 71. NOTAMs convey temporary or time-sensitive operational changes and hazards. Review departure, destination, alternates, route, navigation, and airspace notices, including applicable restrictions. Check current effective times rather than assuming a notice found yesterday remains valid today. Gouge: NOTAM (D) (distant), FDC (regulatory, procedures, TFRs), pointer, military, SAA. FAA NOTAM search, Flight Service, ForeFlight. Required review under 91.103. Mike: asks about current airport conditions and that day’s NOTAMs (e.g. a closed runway). Check them before the checkride.
NOTAMS are included in the standard private pilot weather briefing: True or False?

Generally true: a standard Flight Service briefing includes pertinent NOTAM information within the service's briefing scope. However, do not assume every automated or app-generated weather package contains every relevant notice. Verify the package scope and separately review applicable airport, route, airspace, and restriction information. Responsibility for complete preflight planning remains with the PIC.
Rain on the windshield: what illusion?
Can make you think you’re higher than you are, so you fly a lower approach.
Runway looks farther away: tendency to fly a low approach.
Narrower or wider than usual runway: what illusion?
Narrow: you feel high and fly low. Wide: you feel low and fly high.
Upsloping or downsloping runway: what illusion?
Upslope: you feel high and fly low. Downslope: you feel low and fly high.
During a go-around, what would be the effect if a pilot were to fail to retract the flaps to the go-around setting, leaving them at the full-down position?

Leaving full flaps can create excessive drag, reduce acceleration and climb, and prevent obstacle clearance. Apply the approved power and pitch and retract flaps to the specified go-around setting in the proper sequence. Abruptly retracting all flaps can also cause a dangerous loss of lift. Follow the aircraft's procedure.
During a go-around, what would be the effect of flying the aircraft at an airspeed higher than that recommended in the go-around procedure?

Flying faster than the recommended go-around/obstacle speed can reduce climb angle, increase the distance needed to clear obstacles, and delay appropriate configuration changes. It may also exceed flap limits. Use the POH speed for the phase and objective; best angle, best rate, and acceleration requirements are different.
What would be the effect if the pilot were to allow the aircraft to stall while in a full slip (as during a slip-to-landing maneuver)?

A stall in a slip is still a stall and may include a wing drop, yaw, or progression toward a spin depending on the aircraft and control inputs. Do not teach that a slipping stall is harmless or cannot spin. Maintain an adequate angle-of-attack margin and follow POH slip restrictions. Recover by reducing angle of attack and using the approved procedure.
What oil does your airplane use? What does the W mean?

Check the POH. Training airplanes typically use ashless-dispersant oil (e.g. 15W-50 / 20W-50 multigrade, or AeroShell W-series straight weight). “W” products are ashless dispersant. Steve: and the minimum oil quantity. Gouge: POH says 5 qt minimum (applicant said 6). He checks POH familiarity.

For the checkride airplane: horizontally opposed, air-cooled, 4-cylinder, normally aspirated, carbureted or fuel-injected; horsepower; know it from POH Sec 7. Dave: powerplant: what is direct drive (prop bolted to the crankshaft, no gearbox)? Tell about the propeller: fixed-pitch, aluminum alloy (check the POH).
What safety/emergency equipment is in the airplane?
