Seat belts and shoulder harnesses, fire extinguisher, first aid kit, ELT, and any survival gear for the flight. Mike (11/17): survival gear: there’s no list in the POH, so don’t dig for one. Think it through: blanket, coat, fire starter, food and water to last until rescue, signaling gear.
(Shows a picture of an airplane at night.) Which way is it banking?
Read the attitude indicator: the bank pointer and the horizon relative to the fixed miniature airplane. Mike says 9 out of 10 students get it wrong.
Deviation, Variation, Magnetic dip, Oscillation, Northerly turning error, Acceleration error. Mike only had the first couple explained.

sections.intro: From the Blitz PPL mock oral.
qs: What makes an aircraft airworthy? If AAV1ATE is complied with, is it always airworthy?

It must conform to its approved type design, including applicable alterations and ADs, and be in a condition for safe operation. A current inspection sticker or airworthiness certificate alone does not prove both conditions are met. Review the records and perform a proper preflight. Gouge: No. Airworthy = conforms to its type design (TCDS, STCs, approved alterations) and is in condition for safe operation. Required equipment must work (91.205, KOEL/equipment list, 91.213 for inop items) and the PIC decides on preflight.
Who determines whether the airplane is safe to fly?

The owner/operator is primarily responsible for maintaining airworthiness. The PIC is responsible for determining whether the airplane is in condition for safe flight and must discontinue a flight when unairworthy mechanical, electrical, or structural conditions occur. A maintenance release does not remove the PIC’s responsibility.
When is a 100-hour inspection required for flight instruction?

It applies when a person gives flight instruction for hire in an aircraft that person provides. It also applies to specified carriage of persons for hire. A genuinely independently obtained rental aircraft and separately hired instructor is a different fact pattern; a packaged or affiliated arrangement requires careful evaluation. Do not assume every rental needs a 100-hour or that separate invoices defeat the rule.
Can you exceed a 100-hour inspection limit?

By no more than 10 hours only while en route to a place where the inspection can be performed. The excess time counts toward the next 100 hours. This is not a routine training grace period and does not extend an annual inspection.
Can an annual replace a 100-hour inspection?

Yes, an annual can satisfy the 100-hour requirement. A 100-hour does not replace an annual unless performed by a person authorized to perform annual inspections and entered as an annual. Track both calendar and time-in-service requirements.
What is an Airworthiness Directive, and where do you find one?

An AD is a legally enforceable rule addressing an unsafe condition in an aircraft or product. Search the FAA Dynamic Regulatory System and evaluate applicability to the airframe, engine, propeller, and installed appliances. Verify maintenance records for the required compliance method, recurring interval, and next due status. Mike (11/17): recurring ADs in the maintenance binder.
Can you fly with inoperative equipment?

Only after applying the correct process. If an approved MEL applies, follow it. For an eligible aircraft using 91.213(d), determine that the item is not required by type-design rules, the equipment list/KOEL for the operation, 91.205 or another operating rule, or an AD; then properly remove or deactivate and placard it, accomplish required maintenance/records, and determine it presents no hazard. If requirements are not met, repair it or obtain appropriate authorization. Gouge: Check 91.205 (VFR day: no AI required), the type certificate/KOEL/equipment list, and ADs. If not required: 91.213(d), remove or deactivate it, placard it INOPERATIVE, and record it in the maintenance records as needed.
What would you do if you found fluid near a wheel during preflight?

Identify the source rather than guessing from color alone. Inspect for brake-system leakage, tire/strut problems, and other causes using approved procedures. Do not depart with an unexplained leak or suspect brake condition. Obtain qualified maintenance evaluation and any required repair and approval before flight.
Does alternator failure normally stop a magneto-equipped engine?

Usually not: conventional magnetos produce ignition independently of the alternator and battery. However, electrically dependent ignition, fuel pumps, instruments, or other systems can change the consequences. Know the actual installation. Battery endurance is limited, so follow the failure checklist, shed appropriate loads, and select a suitable landing option. Steve: alternator fails: does the engine still run? Does the prop still spin? Mike (11/17): if the alternator is lost, what powers the electrical system? The battery (through the battery contactor). Know the electrical diagram so you answer fast.
What does the ammeter tell you?

It depends on the installation. A center-zero battery ammeter typically shows charge/discharge, while a loadmeter shows alternator output or electrical load. A low-voltage warning, bus voltage, and current indications together help identify a problem. Know normal indications and failure cues for your aircraft rather than applying one gauge interpretation to every panel. Mike (11/17): ammeter showing an excessive rate of charge: what do you do? Turn off the ALT side of the split master (left half on a Cessna), reduce load. He walks you to it: what controls the lights? The master. What do you do to the master? There are two switches.
What is your first action after an engine failure shortly after takeoff?

Immediately establish the appropriate pitch/airspeed to maintain control and preserve a safe angle of attack. Select a reachable landing area. Use the aircraft’s immediate actions and checklist as time permits; communicate only after control and landing priorities. A useful memory aid is Airspeed, Best landing option, Checklist. Exact speed and shutdown/restart actions come from the POH. Mike: emergency landing scenario: he liked referring to the checklist.
Would you turn back to the runway after a low-altitude engine failure?

Do not assume a turnback is available. It needs adequate altitude, position, wind conditions, performance, and demonstrated proficiency, with a plan established before departure. At low altitude a reachable area generally ahead may be the safer choice. There is no universal turnback altitude valid for every airplane, airport, and pilot.
What are the five hazardous attitudes and their antidotes?

Anti-authority: follow the rules; they usually exist for a reason. Impulsivity: slow down and think. Invulnerability: it could happen to me. Macho: taking chances is foolish. Resignation: I can make a difference. Recognize the attitude in a real decision, then deliberately apply the corrective thought.
Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion/Eating.
Acute vs chronic stress and fatigue?
Acute: short-term, fixed by rest. Chronic: builds over time; needs longer recovery; don’t fly.

Pilot, Aircraft, enVironment, and External pressures. Evaluate yourself, aircraft capability/condition, weather/terrain/airspace, and schedule/passenger pressures. Set practical mitigations or cancel. Personal minimums should be chosen before pressure builds and should reflect actual proficiency, not just legal weather limits.
How do you use a prognostic chart?

Check its issue time, valid time, geographic coverage, and legend. Identify forecast fronts, pressure systems, precipitation, and other features shown by that product. Compare multiple valid times to assess change, then combine the broad forecast with airport and route-specific weather. A prog chart is a forecast, not proof of conditions currently outside. Gouge: Front symbols and weather with each (cold: narrow band of showers/TS, quick clearing; warm: wide area of stratus, rain, low ceilings). Close isobars = strong winds. High = sinking air, clockwise, generally good weather; low = rising air, counterclockwise, clouds and precip. Mike: fronts.
Why are maintenance records and backups important?

They establish inspection status, AD compliance, alterations, component times, and maintenance history. Missing records can make airworthiness status difficult or expensive to establish and can reduce resale value. Organized digital backups help preserve access, but they must be complete and accurate; a scan does not cure missing required content or signatures.
What should you do when you do not know an oral-exam answer?

State what you know, avoid inventing details, and identify the authoritative source you would consult. Demonstrate how you would reach a safe decision. Immediate-action knowledge, aircraft limitations, and practical risk judgment still need to be available when time does not permit research.
You’re lost. What do you do?
5 Cs: Climb, Communicate, Confess, Comply, Conserve. Use VOR, GPS, ATC flight following/radar help.
Walk me through your flight plan with NWKRAFT, PAVE and IMSAFE. Who makes the final go/no-go decision?
Alternator failure near KLGU. Land in a field, go back to KOGD, or land at KLFU?
Land at KLGU (nearest suitable airport). Not a field.
Weather go/no-go scenarios out of KOGD.
He wants good ADM, not regs: if anything goes bad, go land.

sections.intro: Steve’s profile: first leg of the cross-country to the Brigham VOR, then a diversion to Preston for maneuvers, VOR tracking back to Logan, then three landings. Private ACS: altitude ±100 ft, heading ±10°, airspeed ±10 kt.
qs: First cross-country leg to the Brigham VOR.

On course, checkpoints, ETA, fuel check. Mike: soft-field takeoff, start a timer and compare your time to the first checkpoint with the nav log. He may change checkpoints (e.g. just north of the Ogden Delta, the power station, then Brigham). Mike: changes the first two checkpoints (north of Ogden / edge of the Delta, then the power station). Soft or short field takeoff; start the timer (may be midfield downwind) and he’ll ask your time.
Prompt decision, estimate heading, distance, time, fuel; fly it.
Altitude ±100 ft, heading ±10°, airspeed +10/−0 kt, bank ±10°. Mike: climbing and descending turns to specific headings.
Recover promptly and correctly by reference to instruments. Foggles direct to the power station, climb to 8,000–8,500. May ask you to dial up a VOR, find the radial, switch CDI from GPS to VOR.
Recognize and recover promptly; heading ±10°. Mike: power-off stall straight into a power-on stall, after slow flight with turns at 8,500. To the buffet, in very quick succession.
45° ±5° bank, altitude ±100 ft, airspeed ±10 kt, rollout ±10°.
Emergency landing (simulated engine failure) and engine fire.

Best glide, field selection, checklist, communication; engine fire checklist from memory. Mike: ammeter reads negative over Brigham → POH checklist → then an electrical fire → emergency descent → emergency landing at Brigham with a big forward slip. Gouge fail: from 8,500 over the field, extending the pattern took the applicant out of gliding distance → go-around → fail. Stay close (circle down), don’t extend. Land beyond/within the 1,000-footers. Recheck was from midfield downwind.
S-turns or turns around a point (applicant’s choice).
Altitude ±100 ft, airspeed ±10 kt, correct wind correction. Mike: turns around a point at the Maverick gas station sign or south of Brigham.
Track the VOR back to Logan using the CDI.
Tune, identify, intercept and track the radial.

Short field: touchdown at or within 200 ft beyond the point. Soft field: minimum ground speed, weight off the nosewheel. Mike: slip to land, short field hit your point (Brigham), short field takeoff, soft field landing into KOGD keeping the nose up.
Radio calls between maneuvers, even when rushed.
Make every call; don’t skip them to move faster.
Clearing turns and configuration between maneuvers.
Clearing turns even if the examiner says it’s clear; set up cruise configuration before the next maneuver (don’t stay in climb config after power-on stalls).
Talk through corrections and explain the maneuvers.
Call out corrections and why (your error, wind, turbulence, thermals). Be able to explain each maneuver and its ACS standards.
Crosswind control positions while taxiing, taking off and landing.
Correct aileron and rudder for the wind throughout.
Power pulled right after takeoff (engine failure on climb-out).
Pitch for best glide, land straight ahead on remaining runway if possible. Mike then called a go-around.
Prompt power, pitch, configuration cleanup per POH, stay on centerline.
Take your time, don’t leave the tow bar on. He may keep his door open on taxi: challenge it (he liked that).

sections.intro: Steve opens with “Why are you getting an instrument rating?” then goes straight to currency. Mike only glanced at the knowledge test report. Steve cares a lot about regs and where you found the answer (FAR/AIM, faa.gov). It’s open book, but too much searching tells him you’re not prepared.
qs: What do you need to be eligible for this checkride? (paperwork, IACRA, endorsements)

Private cert; 50 hr XC PIC (10 in airplanes); 40 hr actual/simulated instrument (15 with a CFII); 3 hr instrument training in the 2 calendar months before the test; 250 nm IFR XC with an approach at each airport, 3 different approach types; knowledge test within 24 calendar months; endorsements.
Review each ACS code on the report; instructor endorses that deficient areas were covered. Have your missed questions looked up ahead of time; he goes over them and doesn’t want you searching.
Why get an instrument rating? When is one required?
Safety and utility. Required to act as PIC under IFR, in weather below VFR minimums, in Class A, and for SVFR at night.
How do you stay IFR current?
“6 HITS”: 6 approaches, Holding, Intercepting and Tracking courses within the preceding 6 calendar months. Airplane, FFS, FTD or ATD.
Why does the reg say “intercepting and tracking”? Wouldn’t you always do that?
Mike’s answer: some approaches aren’t pilot-navigated. ASR (non-precision) and PAR (precision) are flown on ATC headings/altitudes. Know both terms.
More than 6 months, not current. Now what?
No IFR as PIC. You have 6 more calendar months to get current with a safety pilot (VMC), instructor, or sim/ATD.
IPC with a CFII, examiner or other authorized person, using ACS tasks. Can’t regain with a safety pilot.
At least a private certificate with the category/class rating, a medical (required crewmember), adequate forward/side vision, dual controls (or 91.109 exceptions). Log their name.
Privileges and limitations of the instrument rating?
PIC under IFR or below VFR mins; Class A with clearance and equipment.
Actual or simulated conditions, location and type of each approach, safety pilot name if simulated.

sections.intro: Steve walked the avionics, 91.103, and the required equipment list. Mike made the applicant open the POH for the electrical system and batteries. Know the checkride airplane cold.
qs: Brief me on the avionics in this airplane.
GPS model and whether WAAS, which approaches it can fly (LPV, LNAV/VNAV, LNAV), autopilot modes, backups. Knows where the AFMS supplement is.
What does 91.103 require before an IFR flight?
All available info: weather reports/forecasts, fuel requirements, alternates, known ATC delays, runway lengths, takeoff/landing performance.
How do you find known ATC delays (91.103)?
Flight Service briefing, the FAA ATCSCC NAS Status page (nasstatus.faa.gov), NOTAMs, and ATC.
91.205(d): Generator/alternator, Radios for the route, Altimeter (sensitive), Ball, Clock, Attitude, Rate of turn, Directional gyro (+ DME/RNAV at FL240+). Plus day/night VFR items.
Do you need an attitude indicator? A clock?
Yes, gyroscopic pitch and bank. Clock showing hours, minutes and seconds with a sweep-second pointer or digital display (can be in the avionics).

AAV1ATE: Airworthiness directives, Annual (12 cal months), VOR check (30 days, IFR), 100-hour (for hire or flight instruction in an airplane you provide), Altimeter and pitot-static (24 cal months, IFR in controlled airspace), Transponder (24 cal months), ELT (12 cal months, battery).
VOT ±4°, ground checkpoint ±4°, airborne checkpoint ±6°, dual VOR ±4° between them. Log date, place, error, signature.
Something is inop. Can you go?
91.213: MEL if you have one; otherwise check the equipment list/KOEL, 91.205, ADs; then remove or deactivate and placard.
High-voltage annunciation or ammeter reading high. What do you do?

POH checklist: cycle/turn off the alternator field, reduce load, monitor volts/amps, tell ATC. Second gouge: tell ATC, troubleshoot, probably turn off the alternator because of fire risk. Mike: ammeter showing a really positive charge.
Urgent: load shed, tell ATC, head for nearest VMC or approach while the battery lasts. Know battery endurance from the POH.
What powers your PFD/MFD and standby if the alternator quits? Is there a backup for the PFD?
Main battery, standby/emergency battery, G5 internal battery. Gouge: no backup for the PFD except the G5.
(Preflight) What are those small wicks on the wings and tail?
Static wicks. Bleed off precipitation static, reducing radio/nav interference.
You’re climbing, IAS decreasing, VSI reads zero, altimeter frozen. What’s wrong? (pitot-static failures)

Pitot ram + drain blocked: ASI acts like an altimeter. Static blocked: altimeter frozen, VSI zero, ASI low climbing/high descending. Alternate static reads slightly high. Mike: also asked separately: pitot tube freezes → pitot heat (ASI acts like an altimeter if ram and drain are blocked). Static port freezes → alternate static.
Gyroscopic instruments and AHRS: principles, power, errors.
Rigidity in space, precession. Vacuum vs electric. Know your AHRS.
Air data + attitude heading reference system: computes airspeed, altitude, vertical speed and OAT (air data) and attitude/heading (AHRS) for the PFD.
How do the AHRS sensors work: MEMS gyros, accelerometers, magnetometer?

Solid-state MEMS gyros sense rotation rate in pitch, roll and yaw; accelerometers sense acceleration and gravity to keep the attitude from drifting; the magnetometer senses Earth's magnetic field for heading. The air data computer adds airspeed, altitude and vertical speed from the pitot-static system (ADAHRS = air data + AHRS).
GRABCARD needs a clock. Does your iPad count?

91.205(d) requires a clock with hours, minutes and seconds (sweep-second or digital), installed in the airplane. An iPad isn't installed equipment, so it doesn't meet it; the G1000/G5 or panel clock does.
Variation, deviation, dip: acceleration (ANDS), turning (UNOS), oscillation.
Altimeter within 75 ft of field elevation, ASI 0, AI erect within 5 min, HI matches compass, turn coordinator/ball correct, VSI 0, compass swings freely.
Know the AFMS. ACS requires autopilot use on at least one approach.
Battery dies too. What still works? Can you still navigate with no GPS?

Gouge airplane: the G5s (own batteries) and the pitot-static instruments keep working; GPS, VOR, radios and transponder don’t. Yes, you can still aviate with the G5s, and navigate with an iPad. Know this for your checkride airplane. Mike: how long does the airplane’s battery last? Can you navigate without the G1000?
How long does the G5 battery last?
About 4 hr; check the G5 AFMS.
If the G5s die, can you still fly?
Yes: airspeed, altimeter, VSI and turn coordinator (partial panel).
Do the G5s use one AHRS or two?
Each G5 has its own AHRS.
Can you use an expired GPS database en route? On an approach?

En route: generally yes if you verify waypoints against current charts. Approaches: most Garmin AFMS limitations require a current database, and AFMS limitations are regulatory (91.9). Gouge answer was “FAA yes, Garmin no.” Check your AFMS.

sections.intro: Steve wants the briefing walked through with the prog chart. On icing he asked for the temperature (+5°C), not the types. Mike only asked about the thunderstorm.
qs: Did you get a weather briefing? Walk me through it.
Approved source. METARs, TAFs, GFA, PIREPs, winds aloft, NOTAMs, TFRs, tied to the route.
Explain the prog chart. What’s happening here?

Fronts, pressure centers, precip type/area, IFR/MVFR shading, valid time, and what it means for the route. Pressure systems: highs = sinking air, generally good weather, clockwise flow; lows = rising air, clouds and precip, counterclockwise. Mike: went over the surface analysis chart.
Read the surface analysis chart: what are you looking at?
Observed surface conditions: highs and lows, fronts (types by symbol and color), isobars (tight = strong wind), troughs and ridges, and station models with wind, temp/dew point and pressure.
What is an AIRMET? What are Sierra, Tango and Zulu?

Advisory of weather hazardous to light aircraft. Sierra: IFR and mountain obscuration. Tango: moderate turbulence, sustained surface winds over 30 kt, LLWS. Zulu: moderate icing and freezing level. Issued every 6 hr.
Severe icing, severe or extreme turbulence, dust or sandstorms lowering visibility below 3 sm, volcanic ash. Applies to all aircraft.
Thunderstorms: embedded, lines, areas of severe TS, tornadoes, hail 3/4 in or larger. Issued hourly at H+55. Implies severe turbulence, icing and LLWS.
Center weather advisory: a short-term nowcast from the ARTCC weather unit (CWSU) for conditions happening now or within 2 hr.
At what temperature can icing occur?
Visible moisture at about +5°C or colder (Steve’s answer). Most likely 0 to −20°C. Can form slightly above 0°C from airframe cooling.
Light rain, 10°C on the ground, clouds at 11,000 ft. Would you go?

With about 2°C per 1,000 ft, the freezing level is roughly 5,000 ft above the surface, so the clouds and any precip above that are icing risk. Check freezing level, AIRMET Zulu and PIREPs; plan to stay below the freezing level or don’t go.
What is the standard temperature lapse rate?

Clear (large drops, convective), rime (small drops, stratiform), mixed. Trace/light/moderate/severe. Freezing rain = warmer air above. Induction ice. Mike: which type is most dangerous? Clear ice (and freezing rain/SLD): it forms fast, spreads back past protected areas and is hard to see.
You pick up ice. What do you do? Are you approved for known icing?

Get out: climb/descend/turn toward warmer air or out of moisture, pitot heat and defrost on, extra airspeed, avoid flap changes, tell ATC, PIREP. Training airplanes are not FIKI. Second gouge: full throttle to speed up, disconnect the autopilot, decrease AOA, communicate. Why is ice bad? Increases stall speed. Third gouge: add power, carb heat, pitot heat, reduce AOA. Landing with ice: carry extra speed and land faster (check the POH on flaps).
(Draws a thunderstorm across your route.) How do you know where storms are? What do you do?

Convective SIGMETs/outlook, radar (NEXRAD in cockpit is delayed), satellite, PIREPs, ATC. Avoid by 20 nm, request deviation, never under the anvil or between cells. Go around it, even through the MOA; ask ATC for vectors and help; fly to blue sky. Mike: request radar vectors around it and stay 20 nm away.
Moisture, unstable air, lifting. Cumulus, mature, dissipating. Turbulence, hail, icing, lightning, wind shear, IFR, altimeter errors.
Decode METARs and TAFs. What’s a SPECI?
TAF valid 24 or 30 hr. SPECI when criteria change (e.g. ceiling through 1,000/500 ft).
Standard, abbreviated, outlook. In flight: ATC, FSS, ATIS/ASOS/AWOS, FIS-B (strategic only).
Radiation, advection, upslope, precipitation-induced, steam. Temp/dew point spread.
What type of clouds do we have today, and why? (It was raining.)
Steady rain with low ceilings → stratiform clouds (stable air). Showers → cumuliform (unstable).

sections.intro: Steve’s scenario: KOGD → KBOI, weather provided the day before. Mike’s: KOGD → KRNO on victor airways with VOR checkpoints and MEAs. Student arrives with it done.
qs: Walk me through your route. Would you fly it today?
Route, altitudes vs MEA/MOCA/OROCA, terrain, weather, NOTAMs, TFRs, fuel, personal minimums. Makes a real go/no-go call. Mike: flight plan to KRNO.
Do you need to file an alternate? Why?
1-2-3: from 1 hr before to 1 hr after ETA, destination ceiling ≥ 2,000 and vis ≥ 3 sm, or you need one. Also needed if the destination has no IAP.

Precision 600-2, non-precision 800-2. No IAP: descend from MEA and land VFR. ▲A = non-standard, may apply only to certain approaches/runways; NA = can’t be used. Know where to find them: TPP Alternate Minimums section or ForeFlight. Mike: also asked about non-standard alternate minimums.
Your alternate has no instrument approach. What do you need?
Forecast weather at ETA must allow descent from the MEA, approach and landing under basic VFR.
Can you use GPS/RNAV approaches at the alternate?

RNAV counts as non-precision for planning. WAAS: may plan LNAV/VNAV or LNAV, not LPV (check AIM 1-1-17 and the AFMS). Non-WAAS: if the destination approach is GPS, the alternate needs a non-GPS approach.
Why did you pick that alternate? (KTWF / KLOL)
Weather good enough, usable approach (ILS), fuel range, terrain, services, on or near the route. Mike: he makes you pick one even if the weather is good. Gouge pick: KTRK with the RNAV 20.
Brief the approach at your alternate (KTWF ILS).

Frequencies, FAC, GS intercept altitude, DA, minimums by category, missed, notes. Mike: brief the alternate’s approach (gouge: KTRK RNAV 20). Is it precision or non-precision? Standard precision and non-precision minimums? Can you fly it with current weather? Where’s the FAF?
Destination, then alternate (if required), then 45 min at normal cruise.
What’s in an IFR flight plan and when do you file it?
Aircraft ID/type/equipment, TAS, departure, ETD, altitude, route, destination, ETE, alternate, fuel, POB. At least 30 min before. Mike: how can you file IFR? ATC, Flight Service, ForeFlight, online.

sections.intro: Mike moves the scenario back to Ogden: copy the ATIS and clearance, compute the climb gradient, use the POH climb chart. Steve has the student brief the EMONT THREE.
qs: Runway(s), initial heading/altitude, climb gradient, route to transition, top altitude / expect higher, lost comms notes. Reads the chart fluently.
Do you have to accept a SID?
No. Write “No SID” in the remarks. You still need obstacle clearance on departure (an ODP or other means).
ODP: obstacle clearance only, may be flown without ATC assigning it, graphic or textual. SID: assigned by ATC to simplify clearances and reduce workload; needs a clearance.
Copy this ATIS and clearance, read it back and brief it.
CRAFT: Clearance limit, Route, Altitude (+ expect), Frequency, Transponder. Readback correct.
Holding short of Rwy 3 on C. How do you know you’re at Rwy 3?
Runway holding position sign (red/white), taxiway location sign (black/yellow “C”), hold-short markings.
How do you confirm you’re lined up on Rwy 3?
Heading ≈ 030, runway designator, centerline under you.
200 ft/nm unless published higher. Assumes crossing the departure end at 35 ft and 400 ft before turning.
Can you make the departure’s climb gradient (EMONT 3 from RWY 21)? Show me the math.

fpm = ft/nm × GS ÷ 60. Gouge: 356 ft/nm × 90 kt ÷ 60 ≈ 534 fpm. Then POH climb chart at field elevation, temp and weight. IAS → TAS on the E6B. Second gouge: climb rate at the given temperature, using the altitude at the top of the climb gradient (6,100 MSL). Weather given: calm, 3 sm, OVC042, 40/29, 29.92. Mike: FPM formula; can you make the EMONT 3 on a 40°C day? Work it in the POH.
AIM 5-2-9; TPP climb table; POH Sec 5
After departing on the EMONT 3, how would you enter the hold?
Correct entry from the heading arriving at the holding fix; show it on the chart.
Density altitude on a hot day at KOGD. What changes?
Higher DA, less climb. May need to wait, lighten the load, or use another departure.
You can’t make the climb. ATC denies another departure. Now what?
Request another runway/departure; if denied, VCOA (Visual Climb Over Airport) if weather allows, telling ATC. Or wait / don’t go. Gouge: “Can we do the EMONT 3?” No → VCOA.
Cleared to EMONT then as filed, below the next MEA. Do you have to hold at EMONT to climb?
No, unless an MCA is published. Start climbing right after passing the point where the higher MEA begins.
None required (standard mins are for 121/125/129/135). Know non-standard mins/ODPs.
Void time, hold for release, release time?
Know each. Not off by void time: tell ATC ASAP, no later than 30 min.
Flying the VCOA: what altitude do you cross the VOR at?
Read the route description in the Takeoff Minimums / departure notes at the bottom of the chart. Gouge answer: 8,500 (verify on the current chart).

sections.intro: The core of Steve’s oral. Point at each fix on the student’s route and ask what it is and whether it applies to them.
qs: Talk me through your filed route and why you picked each altitude.
MEA, winds, terrain, O2, direction of flight.
What’s the R flag at KREBS? Does it apply to you?

MRA: lowest altitude to receive the navaids that identify the fix. Only applies if identifying it with VORs. GPS can ID it, but you still meet the MEA. Gouge answer to “do you need to be at that altitude?”: no, because you have an IFR-approved GPS.
Student explains how BLIDA is defined/what LCU refers to on the chart. Examiner: check the current chart.
What’s the X flag at SHEAR? Does it apply to you?
MCA: cross the fix at or above it in the direction shown. Applies to everyone, GPS included (obstacle clearance).
Why is the BYI (Burley VOR) triangle filled in? Lost radar contact over Battle Mountain: do you report?
Compulsory reporting point. Non-radar: report all compulsory points (position, time, altitude, ETA next, next fix). Open triangle = on request. Mike: compulsory reporting points.
What’s the * (MOCA)? Can you fly it?
Obstacle clearance; nav signal only within 22 nm of the VOR. Yes, within 22 nm or if ATC assigns it.
Minimum en route altitude: guarantees obstacle clearance and navigation signal coverage for the whole segment.
What is a MOCA (the * on the chart)? Can you fly it?
Minimum obstruction clearance altitude: obstacle clearance for the segment, but nav signal only within 22 nm of the VOR. You can fly it within 22 nm of the VOR, or when ATC assigns it.
What is an MRA (the R flag)? Does it apply to you?
Minimum reception altitude: lowest altitude where you can receive the navaids that identify an intersection. Only matters if you’re identifying the fix with VORs; an IFR-approved GPS can identify it.
What is an MCA (the X flag)? Does it apply to you?
Minimum crossing altitude: cross the fix at or above it in the direction shown, usually before climbing to a higher MEA. Applies to everyone, GPS included.
Maximum authorized altitude: the highest usable altitude on the segment (above it you may get interference from other navaids).
What is an OROCA? When would you use it?

Off-route obstruction clearance altitude: 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle in the grid (2,000 ft in mountainous areas). No nav signal guarantee. Useful when you’re off an airway, e.g. lost comms on a deviation.
Where you switch from one navaid to the next on an airway, shown as a Z-like symbol with the mileages. Usually midway unless charted otherwise.
What’s a victor airway? A T-route (tango)?
Victor: VOR-based low-altitude airways, 1,200 AGL up to (not including) 18,000 MSL, 4 nm each side of centerline. T-routes: low-altitude RNAV (GNSS) routes.
Air route traffic control center: provides ATC for IFR traffic en route between terminal areas.
Thunderstorm ahead; ATC offers a deviation through an MOA and a restricted area. Can you go?
Yes, if ATC clears you through (area inactive or coordinated).
Reports to make without being asked?

MARVELOUS VFR C500: Missed, Airspeed ±10 kt/5%, Reaching hold, Vacating altitude, ETA ±2 min, Leaving hold, Outer marker, Unforecast wx, Safety of flight, VFR-on-top change, FAF, Radio/nav failure, Compulsory points, 500 fpm unable.
How does a VOR work? What are the service volumes?
Ground station transmits 360 radials; receiver shows your radial from the station. Service volumes: Terminal, Low and High (newer VL/VH), each with its own range and altitude.
What does DME give you? What is slant range error?
Distance to the station along a straight line (slant range). Error is greatest close to the station at high altitude; negligible when 1 nm or more away for each 1,000 ft of altitude.
Receiver measures distance (time) to multiple satellites and computes position. Needs 3 satellites for 2D, 4 for 3D.
Receiver autonomous integrity monitoring: the receiver checks satellite integrity using extra satellites (5 for fault detection, 6 to exclude a bad one). Check RAIM prediction preflight for non-WAAS.
Wide area augmentation system: ground stations and geostationary satellites correct GPS errors and add integrity, allowing LPV and LNAV/VNAV approaches.
You lose RAIM. What do you do?

Don’t rely on GPS for navigation; revert to other nav (VOR, radar vectors) and tell ATC. On an approach before the FAF, don’t continue; after the FAF, go missed if RAIM is lost for over 5 minutes or as the box directs.
What are the IFR cruising altitudes?
Below 18,000 MSL: magnetic course 0–179° odd thousands; 180–359° even thousands.
Minimum IFR altitude when no MEA applies?
2,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 4 nm of course in mountainous areas; 1,000 ft elsewhere.
Airspace VFR weather mins; special use airspace.
Table by class. MOA vs restricted vs prohibited.

sections.intro: Mike spends real time here as a chained scenario off the route. Steve hinted at it in the air (“Expect further clearance in 5 minutes” at the RACGO hold).
qs: You lose comms in VMC. What do you do?
Squawk 7600, stay VFR, land as soon as practicable, tell ATC. Nearest suitable airport. Mike: back in VFR conditions after losing comms: stay VFR and land as soon as practicable.
Lose comms in IMC. What route?
AVEF: Assigned, Vectored (direct to the fix/route vectored toward), Expected, Filed. Mike: scenario on your KRNO trip: lose comms at a given spot, using the CRAFT clearance he gave you.
Highest of MEA, Expected, Assigned, recomputed each segment.
You lose comms while off route on a weather deviation. Now what altitude?
Most direct route back to the cleared route at a safe altitude. Gouge: Mike accepted climbing to the OROCA, since MEAs only apply on the airway. Name the altitude.
Deviating around a thunderstorm through a restricted area, you lose comms. VFR? IFR?

VMC: squawk 7600, stay VFR, leave the restricted area by the most direct route, land as soon as practicable. IMC: you were cleared through, so continue per 91.185 (AVEF route, MEA altitude), squawk 7600, and rejoin your route.
When do you leave the clearance limit?
Limit is an IAF: begin descent/approach at or close to ETA (or EFC). Not an IAF: hold until EFC (or arrive), then go to an IAF.
Holding at RACGO, “expect further clearance in 5 minutes,” radios die. Now what?
7600, keep holding at assigned altitude, leave at the EFC and fly the expected approach (VOR-A into Ogden).
Lost comms right after takeoff on the EMONT THREE?
Follow the DP’s lost comms notes, then AVEF / MEA.
Other freqs, 121.5, cell phone, light gun signals, VOR voice, ident.

sections.intro: Mike gave a hold on the ground using a radial (applicant drew it and named a parallel entry) and in the air using a bearing. Drill both.
qs: Copy this hold. Draw it. Which entry? What goes in the GPS?
70° line for direct/parallel/teardrop. Radial = FROM, inbound is the reciprocal. Bearing = TO, inbound matches. Gouge: ZESER NW on the 130 bearing → inbound 130. Mike: draws a hold before the flight.
Direction from fix, fix, radial/course/bearing/airway, leg length if non-standard, left turns if non-standard, EFC.
1 min inbound ≤14,000 MSL, 1.5 above. Triple the inbound WCA outbound.
What do you report in a hold?
Time and altitude reaching the fix; leaving the fix.
Hold-in-lieu-of-PT: when do you fly it?
Required unless straight-in, NoPT, vectored to final or timed approach. One circuit unless cleared otherwise.
You go missed at KBOI. How do you enter the missed approach hold?
Correct entry from heading arriving at the holding fix, shown on the chart.
What’s the most important thing while you’re in a hold?

Not answered in the gouge. Strong answers: stay in protected airspace (correct entry, timing, wind correction, speed) and know your EFC. Mike: if ATC tells you to hold, what should you be worried about? Your fuel.

sections.intro: Steve: SPUD FOUR into KBOI, RNAV X/Y/Z, LPV vs LNAV with a drawing. Mike: AIM 5-4-5 is his go-to; FAF on the ILS is a trap question.
qs: Transitions, starting fix, published altitudes/speeds, expect vs mandatory, where it ends, landing-direction notes. Can you refuse a STAR? “No STAR” in remarks. Gouge: “cleared to descend via from BROPH”: comply with the published altitude and speed restrictions from BROPH on.
What does “proceed to Boise landing west” mean?
Descend via: lateral + published altitude/speed restrictions. Cleared via: lateral only, maintain assigned altitude.
Why are there RNAV (GPS) X, Y and Z approaches to the same runway?
Same guidance type, different procedures: minimums, segments, equipment or missed. Letters start at Z. Read the notes.
Of the RNAV (GPS) X, Y and Z to 28R, which can you fly in our airplane, and why?

Look at the notes and equipment requirements on each plate: one may require RNP/RF legs or special authorization (RNP AR) your GPS can't do. Fly the version whose requirements your avionics meet (WAAS GPS, LPV/LNAV), and brief the missed and its hold.
KBOI RNAV (GPS) Y 28R: where do you go after CANEK, and at what altitude?
Read it off the plan view and profile; brief the segment and altitude.
Can you fly the missed in your airplane?
Missed climb gradient vs airplane performance at KBOI elevation/temp.
What is an LPV approach? What does it look like?
WAAS-based approach with vertical guidance. Angular like an ILS: the course narrows toward the runway. Flown to a DA.
What is an LNAV approach? What does it look like?
Lateral guidance only, linear (±0.3 nm full scale on final), step-downs to an MDA.
Lateral plus vertical guidance from WAAS or approved baro-VNAV, flown to a DA. An APV, not precision.
LNAV vs LP: what's the difference?

Both are lateral only, flown to an MDA. LP uses WAAS for angular (localizer-like) lateral guidance that tightens toward the runway, so it often has lower minimums; LNAV is linear (±0.3 nm full scale) and doesn't need WAAS. LP and LPV aren't published on the same approach.
ILS, PAR and GLS: lateral and vertical guidance meeting precision standards, flown to a DA.
What is an APV, and which approaches are APVs?
Approach with vertical guidance that doesn’t meet precision standards: LPV and LNAV/VNAV. Flown to a DA.
LP, LNAV, LOC, VOR, NDB, ASR: lateral guidance only, flown to an MDA.
KTWF ILS 26: going direct to STRIK on your own nav, do you need the procedure turn?
Yes, fly the PT or hold-in-lieu unless the route is marked NoPT or ATC clears you straight-in.
Vectored to final: do you fly the procedure turn?
When don’t you fly a procedure turn?
NoPT route, straight-in clearance, radar vectors to final, or a timed approach from a hold.
Locator outer marker (an NDB at the outer marker); initial approach fix.
Where is the FAF on an ILS?
Trap question: where you intercept the glideslope at the published intercept altitude (lightning bolt), not the Maltese cross. The Maltese cross is the FAF for the localizer-only approach.
Where's the MAP on the ILS? On the LOC?
ILS: the DA on the glideslope is the missed approach point (decide there). LOC: the MAP is shown on the profile: a fix, DME or timing from the FAF using the table at the bottom of the plate.
How does temperature move that GS intercept point?
Hot: higher than indicated, intercept farther out. Cold: lower than indicated, intercept closer.
Cold temperature airports: what and what do you do?
Snowflake icon with a temperature. At or below it, correct altitudes on the marked segments and tell ATC.
DA vs MDA at the missed approach point?
DA: decide at DA; momentary descent below while going missed is OK. MDA: level off, never go below it.
When do you have to be stabilized?
By 1,000 ft above TDZE in IMC (500 VMC): on speed, on path, configured, normal descent rate.
What do you need to descend below DA/MDA? Name the visual references.

(1) Continuously in position to land normally; (2) flight vis ≥ published; (3) a visual reference: ALS (100-ft rule unless red bars), threshold, threshold markings/lights, REIL, VASI/PAPI, TDZ/markings/lights, runway/markings/lights. Mike: what 3 things do you need to go below minimums? With the approach lighting system in sight you can descend to 100 ft above TDZE.
What does AIM 1-2-3 let you do with GPS on conventional procedures?

Use a suitable RNAV/GPS system in place of ground navaids: to determine position, fly DME arcs, navigate to/from an NDB or VOR, hold over a navaid, or substitute for ADF/DME on an approach. You can't use it for lateral guidance on the final segment of a conventional approach (LOC, VOR, NDB) unless the approach says 'or GPS.'
Lose sight of the runway while circling?
Climbing turn toward the runway of intended landing, then intercept the missed.
When must you fly the published missed?
When executing a missed unless ATC assigns something else.
What makes you Category A and why? Circling: protected areas and expanded (inverse C) circling.

Category comes from Vref, or 1.3 × Vso if no Vref is given, at max certificated landing weight. Cat A < 91 kt, B 91–120. It’s in the TPP general information/legend. If you circle faster than your category, use the higher category’s mins. Know the TERPS circling radii and the expanded circling symbol.
When can you descend on a segment or a vector?
Only when established on a published segment or cleared for the approach on a published route.

Last point to start a normal descent from MDA. Don’t leave MDA before it. LOC: runway in sight before the VDP → wait until the VDP to descend. Mike: talked about VDPs, and what descent rate you need after a VDP (a normal ~3° path; roughly groundspeed × 5 fpm).

TERM within 30 nm of the airport; LPV (or the line of minima you’re using) annunciated before the FAF. If it doesn’t annunciate, don’t descend on it; fly the missed (or use LNAV mins only if LNAV is annunciated). Mike: GPS should show TERM near the airport.
KRNO: calm, RVR 1800, OVC011, 15/15, 29.92. Cleared for the ILS Z 17R. Can you legally fly it and land?

Read the plate first. Standard minimum is RVR 2400, but the chart note allows RVR 1800 with a flight director, autopilot or HUD to DA. With the G5 flight director or the autopilot, RVR 1800 works. Then 91.175 still applies below DA. The examiner may raise the weather and ask again.
Runway visual range: instrument-measured horizontal distance a pilot can see down the runway from the approach end, in feet. Used for takeoff/landing minimums.
When was this approach plate amended?
Bottom left of the chart (Amdt number and date).
At the MDA you see the white runway lights. Can you descend? Does this approach have red bars?
Yes, but only to 100 ft above TDZE on the approach lights unless red terminating or side-row bars are visible. ALSF has red bars; MALSR doesn’t.
You lose GPS on the missed approach. What do you do?
Tell ATC, use other nav (VOR, vectors), fly the published missed if able. Mike: KRNO ILS 17R circling and you lose GPS on the missed: tell ATC and ask for radar vectors to the hold.
Weather is below minimums at your destination. Now what?
Hold for improvement if fuel allows, or divert to your alternate. Tell ATC.
Missed approach, you’ve already tried once and you have 15 min of fuel left. What do you do?
It’s an emergency: declare, tell ATC, and land as best you can (best available approach or airport). Don’t keep shooting approaches toward fuel exhaustion.

sections.intro: Not on either gouge but fair game in the IR ACS. Run quickly and slow down wherever the student hesitates.
qs: Leans, Coriolis, graveyard spiral, somatogravic; false horizon, autokinesis, black hole, runway width/slope.
What is hypoxia? Types and symptoms?
Not enough oxygen. Hypoxic (altitude), hypemic (CO, anemia), stagnant (circulation), histotoxic (alcohol, drugs). Symptoms: euphoria, headache, impaired judgment, cyanosis, tingling.
Carbon monoxide poisoning: symptoms and what do you do?
Headache, drowsiness, dizziness. Heat off, fresh air, oxygen if available, land.
Acute: short-term, fixed by rest. Chronic: builds over time, needs longer recovery; don’t fly.
Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion/Eating.
8 hr bottle to throttle, under 0.04 BAC, not under the influence.
Above 12,500 to 14,000 MSL: crew after 30 min. Above 14,000: crew always. Above 15,000: provide to occupants.
PAVE, IMSAFE, 3P, 5P, personal minimums, automation management.
Nose high: power up, pitch down, level wings. Nose low: power reduce, level wings, raise nose.
Surface area below 10,000 MSL, clear of clouds, 1 sm, clearance. Night needs IR and IFR airplane.
PIC responsibilities and emergencies in IMC (vacuum/AHRS, electrical, engine)?
Emergency authority, 7700, malfunction reports, nearest suitable, partial panel.
Clearance, ground, tower, approach/departure, ARTCC. “Radar contact” vs “radar contact lost.”
VFR-on-top is an IFR clearance at VFR altitudes. Contact: must be requested, 1 sm, clear of clouds.

sections.intro: Profiles from both gouges. ACS standards: altitude ±100 ft, heading ±10°, airspeed ±10 kt, CDI ≤ ¾ scale on final, MDA +100/−0, no descent below DA without visual references.
qs: Preflight GPS checks: WAAS position and RAIM prediction.
WAAS: Menu > Tools > Info > GPS, check the Fix field shows “3D Position (WAAS)”. RAIM: Menu > Tools > RAIM Prediction, enter destination and time, Compute.
IFR cockpit checks, taxi instrument check, clearance copied and briefed.

Complete, organized, checklist used. Flow: Taxi: ball, altimeters within ±75 ft, heading vs magnetic compass, attitude (blue over brown). Runup: VSI 0, airspeed 0, load KBMC UNICOM and AWOS, heading bug northbound.
Departure: flies the DP/clearance, climb gradient, transition to cruise.

Within standards; correct altitudes and fixes. Flow: Announce engine instruments in the green, Vr 65, Vy 76, turn northbound, set heading/altitude/IAS 82, verify, then engage the autopilot at 800 AGL. Foggles on; climb/cruise checklist.
Unusual attitude recoveries (Steve did them quickly en route).

Correct, prompt recovery, no excessive G or airspeed. Flow: Nose low (brown): power idle, wings level, nose up. Nose high (blue): power in, wings level, nose down. Remember to re-engage the autopilot after unusual attitudes to continue to JOSIF.
Direct KONNE, procedure turn, RNAV 35 into KBMC, circle (wind).

PT flown correctly, approach mode checked, circling within protected area and at MDA. Flow: Build a quick bug brief, frequency 123.05, descent checklist, call 10 sm out “inbound RNAV 35,” set baro mins, fly 90–95 kt, announce 7 sm, 3 sm, and going missed.
Climb, clean up, follow assigned missed, reports.
Hold: RACGO with EFC (lost comms hint) / ZESER NW on the 130 bearing.

Correct entry, timing, wind correction, reports, EFC handling. Flow: Direct RACGO, verify heading and altitude, autopilot on, 121.1. GPS: FPL → select RACGO → hold at waypoint → activate → verify on the map. AP times the legs, you time the 5 min. Announce established, brief the approach, set baro mins. At 5 min: “Contacting approach for the approach clearance… no response, squawk 7600, inbound for the expected approach.” Mike (gouge 4): bad weather: hold-in-lieu-of-PT at JOSIF, cleared for the ILS RWY 3 into Ogden on the inbound.
Correct nav source, step-downs, MDA discipline, circle. Flow: VS descent at 90–95 kt. Missed: climbing left to 5,400, Vy 76. Ogden frequency 121.1.

Stabilized, GS within ¾ scale, DA discipline, safe circle. Flow: Set baro mins, switch to green needles (LOC), partial panel, 90–95 kt, GPS on the map page to see the course, ~500 fpm, DA about 5,000 (check the chart). Circle within 1.3 nm of the airport (Cat A).
ILS briefed and set up, then it's unserviceable: quickly switch to the RNAV 03 at KOGD, take vectors, get cleared and land.
Grades how fast you re-brief and re-load: load the new approach, check minimums and missed, verify the GPS annunciation, then fly it.
ILS with autopilot direct WEGET with PT; slow to 70 kt (notch of flaps), resume speed at descent.
Autopilot managed correctly, takes the published PT, speed control.
Hand-flown localizer into KTVY; missed ~1 mi out with a non-published climb-out.
Hand-flown within standards; follows ATC’s climb-out (left turn northbound).
Partial panel: RNAV 03 KOGD with PFD off, G5 only, no autopilot; circle to RWY 17.
Controls airplane on backup, flies approach within standards, safe circle at normal minimums.
Single-pilot resource management throughout (automation, checklists, ATC comms).
Stays ahead of the airplane; good comms and readbacks.

Second profile: vectors under the hood (autopilot off until 800 AGL), unusual attitudes, ILS 17 at Tooele (KTVY), coordinate the missed, hold, vectors to the LOC, circle; then RNAV at OGD to circling mins.
Within standards throughout; ask when he wants the hood off.

sections.intro: Not on the gouge but standard opening material. Have the logbook, endorsements and knowledge test report ready.
qs: What experience do you need for the commercial certificate (ASEL)?

250 hr total (100 powered, 50 in airplanes); 100 hr PIC (50 in airplanes); 50 hr XC (10 in airplanes); 20 hr training incl. 10 hr instrument, 10 hr complex/TAA/turbine, day and night XC, 3 hr prep within 2 months; 10 hr solo/PIC incl. a 300 nm XC with a 250 nm leg and 5 hr night VFR with 10 takeoffs/landings at a towered airport.
Privileges and limitations of a commercial certificate?

Act as PIC for compensation or hire, and carry persons or property for compensation (subject to Part 119 / operating rules). Without an instrument rating: no carrying passengers for hire on XC over 50 nm or at night.
What medical do you need, and how long is it good for commercial privileges?
Second class: commercial privileges through the end of the 12th month, then reverts to third-class privileges for its remaining duration.
What tells you when you can get paid as a commercial pilot? What can you do for hire without a Part 119 certificate?

119.1(e) exceptions, e.g. student instruction, nonstop sightseeing within 25 sm (with 91.147 LOA), ferry/training flights, aerial work like banner towing, crop dusting, aerial photography and survey (no passengers carried for hire). Gouge 2: “What tells us we can get paid as commercial pilots?” Part 119 (applicability and the 119.1(e) exceptions), along with 61.133.
What do you need to bring to be legal?
Using the maintenance logbooks, when was the last annual?
Find the annual entry and confirm it’s within the preceding 12 calendar months.
When was the last transponder inspection?
100-hour: when was it done and how many hours until the next?
Compute from the tach/hobbs at the last 100-hour. Can be exceeded by up to 10 hours only to reach a place to do it.
ELT: when was it inspected and when is the battery due?
Inspection every 12 calendar months; battery replaced after 1 hr cumulative use or 50% of its useful life.
What are the aircraft’s required documents? (SPARROW)
Supplements, Placards, Airworthiness certificate, Radio station license (international), Registration, Operating limitations, Weight and balance.
Can you fly this flight at night without a landing light? If it’s inop, what do you do?
Yes if not for hire: 91.205(c) only requires a landing light when operating for hire. Deactivate and placard it (91.213).

sections.intro: Steve’s biggest area. He jumps straight into “Is this legal?” scenarios and wants the thought process out loud, not a yes/no: who owns the airplane, who has operational control, who’s paying, is there compensation, holding out, is transportation being sold. Gouge 2: know WHERE to find the answers (AC 120-12A, AC 91-37B, Part 119).
qs: Walk me through how you decide if a flight is Part 91, Part 135, or illegal charter.

Talk it out: Who owns the airplane? Who has operational control? Is compensation involved? Am I holding out? Is transportation being sold? Is it starting to look like charter? Slow down instead of blurting an answer. Steve: he describes his own operation and asks if it’s legal.
Scenario: a developer wants you to fly him and a business associate from OGD to Boise in his airplane. Legal? Can you be paid?

Part 91 corporate/company flying. He owns or leases the airplane and has operational control, there’s no holding out, transportation isn’t being sold, and the flight is incidental to his business. A commercial pilot can be paid to fly for the company. Mike: “Can I pay you to fly me in my plane wherever I want?” Yes, that’s Part 91.
Scenario: he then wants you to fly his wife and kids from Boise to McCall.
Still Part 91: owner/family transportation. No transportation sold, no holding out. Flying family around isn’t automatically charter.
Scenario: he wants you to move contractors for a partner company. Legal?

Stop and think. Who owns the airplane, who has operational control, who’s paying, is transportation becoming a service? Red flags: carrying another company’s people, providing airplane plus pilot, transportation for compensation. Likely a Part 119/135 issue or illegal charter. Key question: “Am I transporting people for hire?”
Scenario: a charity wants you to give rides. Can you?

Don’t answer instantly. Are passengers paying? Are donations tied to rides? Is transportation being sold? Charity + money = investigate. Know 91.146 (charitable/fundraising flights and their conditions). Steve: he makes sure you know you can’t get paid for charity work (know 91.146 and its conditions).
Exercising authority over initiating, conducting or terminating a flight. Who decides where and when to go, which passengers, weather and maintenance calls, and whether the flight happens at all.

Dry lease: airplane only; lessee provides the pilot and has operational control, usually Part 91. Wet lease: airplane plus at least one crewmember; big red flag, looks like transportation for hire, Part 119/135 issue. Gouge 2: which one’s legal? Dry lease is generally legal under Part 91. A wet lease carrying passengers or property for compensation needs a Part 119 certificate (121/135); without one it’s illegal charter. AC 91-37B.
Holding out to the public to carry persons or property for compensation, to anyone who wants it. Needs a Part 119 certificate.
Carrying for compensation for a few select customers under specific arrangements, without holding out.
Advertising or letting it be known you’ll provide transportation for compensation: ads, signs, word of mouth, agents, a reputation.
Where would you find these definitions?
14 CFR 1.1 (operational control), 119.3 (wet lease), AC 120-12A (private vs common carriage, holding out), AC 91-37B (truth in leasing). Steve likes seeing you look them up instead of guessing.

sections.intro: Steve wants you to go straight to the POH charts instead of guessing numbers, and he cares whether a flight is smart, not just legal.
qs: Work this weight and balance problem. Would you actually make the flight with four passengers?
Compute weight and CG from the POH. Even if it’s within limits, a 4-cylinder airplane at high density altitude has thin margins. Conservative decision making is the answer he liked.
What happens if baggage isn’t tied down?
It can shift during takeoff or turbulence and move the CG, possibly out of limits; it can also become a projectile or jam controls. Secure all cargo.
What’s your takeoff roll / climb / runway requirement for this flight?

Go straight to the POH charts and work it out for pressure altitude, temperature, weight and wind. “I’d reference the POH and verify with the charts.” Gouge 2: high density altitude scenario: would you take off? Steve: he writes out a density altitude / wind / performance problem to work with the POH charts.
Density altitude: what is it and what does it do?
Pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature. Hot, high and heavy = longer takeoff roll, less climb, less margin.
Mountain and canyon flying: what are the hazards and how do you handle them?

Density altitude, downdrafts, turbulence, rapidly changing weather, rising terrain. Always leave yourself an out: fly the side of the canyon to allow a turn, cross ridges at an angle with altitude to spare, have an escape route. Gouge 2: what to do around high mountains. Steve: always be cautious; don’t put yourself in dumb situations.
CG too far forward vs too far aft?

Forward: higher stall speed, more elevator needed, harder to flare, slower cruise. Aft: less stable, harder stall/spin recovery. Mike: fuel burn moves CG slightly forward. Forward CG: lower cruise, more fuel burn, longer takeoff, easier stall recovery, higher stall speed.
Taking off downhill on a sloped runway: shorter or longer takeoff distance?
Shorter (gravity helps acceleration). Uphill is longer.
Exceeding the critical angle of attack, at any airspeed or attitude.
The angle between the wing’s chord line and the relative wind.
How do you recover from a stall?
Reduce the angle of attack, level the wings, add power as needed, return to the desired flight path.
How do you recover from a spin?
PARE: Power idle, Ailerons neutral, Rudder full opposite, Elevator forward to break the stall; neutralize rudder when rotation stops and recover from the dive.
How is rudder used with ailerons? What makes the nose point away from the turn?
Rudder simultaneously with aileron when starting the turn. Adverse yaw from the down aileron’s extra drag.
Vx best angle (altitude per distance), Vy best rate (altitude per time).

sections.intro: Steve asked these scenario style: what are you doing if a passenger shows symptoms? Also know the scuba question; it does come up.
qs: Can you fly after scuba diving?

Decompression sickness (“the bends”) risk. Wait at least 12 hr after a dive not requiring a controlled ascent (for flights up to 8,000 ft); 24 hr if flying above 8,000 ft or after a dive that required a controlled ascent.
Above 12,500 to 14,000 MSL: crew after 30 min. Above 14,000: crew the whole time. Above 15,000: each occupant must be provided oxygen.
A passenger shows hypoxia symptoms. What do you do?
Descend, get oxygen on, communicate with ATC, land if needed. Know symptoms: euphoria, headache, impaired judgment, cyanosis, tingling, drowsiness.
How does a pressurization system work? What do you do if you lose pressurization?
Engine bleed/turbo air pumped into the cabin, outflow valve controls cabin altitude. Loss: oxygen masks on, emergency descent, tell ATC. Know time of useful consciousness.
Hypoxic (altitude), hypemic (CO, anemia), stagnant (poor circulation, G-forces), histotoxic (alcohol, drugs).
Passenger gets airsick. What do you do?
Fresh air, cool vents, have them look outside at the horizon, smooth flying, land if needed.

sections.intro: Steve wants understanding, not memorized numbers.
qs: How do magnetos work? Why does the engine keep running with the master switch off?

Magnetos are self-contained, engine-driven generators that make spark independent of the electrical system. Two for redundancy and better combustion. Gouge 2: if you lose electrical, does the engine still run? Yes, the magnetos.
How does a carburetor work? What causes carb ice and what are the symptoms?

Venturi lowers pressure, draws fuel in; fuel vaporization and pressure drop cool the air. Ice is possible from about −7°C to +21°C with visible moisture or high humidity. Symptoms: RPM drop (fixed pitch) or MP drop (constant speed), rough running. Mike: taking off from Ogden, engine roughness on a humid day → carb ice.
Why does carb heat fix it, and what happens when you apply it?
Routes heated, unfiltered air into the carburetor to melt ice. RPM drops further at first (less dense air, and melting ice going through), then rises as ice clears.
Constant-speed propeller: how does it work?
Governor varies blade angle to hold the selected RPM; throttle sets MP. Increase: mixture, prop, throttle. Decrease: throttle, prop, mixture.
Retractable gear: operation, emergency extension, warnings?
Know the system in the checkride airplane (hydraulic/electric), gear warning horn, emergency extension procedure.
Inoperative equipment: where do you find what’s required?

91.205, the airplane’s type certificate / comprehensive equipment list (KOEL), ADs; then 91.213(d): remove or deactivate, placard INOPERATIVE, log it. Steve: Day VFR equipment comes from 91.205 and the type certificate (TCDS). Know how and where to find the TCDS (FAA DRS).
Overvoltage. If the battery dies, does the engine still run? Is it an emergency?
POH overvoltage checklist. Yes, the magnetos keep it running. Not necessarily an emergency.

sections.intro: Steve mixes in a lot of private pilot basics. Be sharp on airspace and weather minimums.
qs: Two-way radio communication established before entering, Mode C transponder and ADS-B Out. Shelf/veil areas: know the dimensions. Gouge 2: who do you contact when approaching Class C? Approach control (frequency on the sectional/Chart Supplement).
When is a transponder (and ADS-B Out) required? Exceptions?

Class A, B and C; within the 30 nm Mode C veil; above 10,000 MSL except at and below 2,500 AGL; above the ceiling of Class B/C up to 10,000. Exceptions for aircraft without electrical systems in some areas.
18,000 MSL up to FL600. IFR only: instrument rating, IFR clearance, transponder and ADS-B.
VFR weather minimums in Class E and G?

E below 10,000: 3 sm, 500 below / 1,000 above / 2,000 horizontal. At/above 10,000: 5 sm, 1,000/1,000/1 sm. G day below 1,200 AGL: 1 sm, clear of clouds. Know the rest of the table. Gouge 2: weather minimums for the various classes of airspace.
B: clearance. C and D: two-way communication. E and G: none (unless towered airport).
3 takeoffs and landings to a full stop, 1 hr after sunset to 1 hr before sunrise, within the preceding 90 days.
Restricted airspace on your route: who controls it, and can you go through?

Only when it’s inactive or the controlling agency authorizes it. Controlling and using agency are in the special use airspace table on the sectional (and the Chart Supplement). Mike: with permission; when inactive you can fly through.
Transponder requirements in Class D? What kind of transponder does your airplane have?
Class D alone doesn’t require a transponder (check 91.215 for the veil and other areas). Find the model in the POH supplement or the panel, then look it up (Garmin): Mode C or Mode S.
What is an MEF? Where do the numbers come from, and where’s the proof?
Maximum elevation figure: highest terrain or man-made obstruction in the quadrangle plus a buffer, rounded up. The sectional legend explains it.
How high above the MEF should you fly?
What’s the top of the Ogden Class D?
Read it off the sectional (the number in the dashed blue box, in hundreds of feet MSL). Check the current chart.
What does Ogden’s airspace become when the tower closes?
Check the Chart Supplement for KOGD. Answers have included both Class E and Class G up to 700 AGL.
Can you fly VFR with 1 mile visibility near Ogden? Where?
Only in Class G (day, at or below 1,200 AGL, clear of clouds), or with a special VFR clearance in the surface area.
What airspace is above the Salt Lake Bravo above 12,000?
Can you fly in Class E above 10,000 MSL with 4 miles visibility?
No. At or above 10,000 MSL (and more than 1,200 AGL) you need 5 sm and 1,000 below, 1,000 above, 1 sm horizontal.
Which aircraft has right of way over every other aircraft?

sections.intro: The planning portion felt straightforward: a ForeFlight brief, weather, the route, and filing IFR.
qs: Walk me through your flight plan and weather briefing.
Route, terrain, weather, performance, alternates. Explain your reasoning. Steve: 91.103 preflight action.
How would you file IFR for this trip?
Route, altitude, alternate if required, fuel, and whether you’d accept it today.
Go/no-go: would you take this flight?
Personal minimums, terrain, density altitude, weather trends. Smart, not just legal. Gouge 2: personal minimums.
At what temperature can you get structural icing?
Gouge answer: icing can happen around 2–5°C, so just avoid visible moisture near freezing. Most likely 0 to −20°C.
Landing, and there’s an airplane only a mile in front of you. Do you land behind it, land in the field next to the runway, or go around?
Go around. (His note: with soft-field experience, the field could work, but a go-around is the answer.)
What is a CWA and when is it issued?
Center weather advisory: issued by the ARTCC weather unit as needed for conditions now or within 2 hr.
What does the surface analysis chart show?
Observed surface conditions: fronts, highs and lows, isobars, station models.
Fronts, temperature inversions, terrain and mountain waves, thunderstorms and microbursts.
How does performance change as the wind changes (shear)?
Headwind that drops off or becomes a tailwind: airspeed drops and you sink. Tailwind becoming a headwind: airspeed and lift increase briefly.
IMSAFE: walk me through it for this flight.
Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion/Eating.
How does PAVE apply to this flight? What external pressures could there be?
Pilot (IMSAFE), Aircraft (AAV1ATE, documents, W&B), enVironment (weather, terrain, airspace), External pressures (passengers, schedule, get-there-itis).
VFR fuel requirement? Minimum legal fuel at takeoff for this flight?
Fuel to the first point of intended landing plus 30 min day (45 night) at normal cruise. Compute it for this flight.
Planned TAS? With a 50 kt headwind, what’s your groundspeed and what changes?
TAS from the POH; GS = TAS − 50. Time and fuel burn go up.
What altitude did you plan and why? Do you legally need an alternate VFR?
VFR cruising altitudes (91.159). No alternate required VFR.
NOTAMs, weather, known delays, thunderstorm distance?
Check NOTAMs and the briefing; known ATC delays (91.103); avoid thunderstorms by 20 mi.
What’s the maximum wind shear you’d fly with?
Personal minimums question: give a conservative number and why.

sections.intro: Steve’s profile: timed to a point, then straight into maneuvers, then landings at Brigham. He asks emergency scenarios while you fly. Know the Commercial ACS tolerances.
qs: Departure (VOR departure / timed to a checkpoint).

On course, ETA within standards, pilotage/dead reckoning. Gouge 2: VOR departure, then maneuvers, emergencies, landings at Brigham, back to OGD. Mike: soft-field takeoff, timed departure to the edge of the Delta then the power station.
Altitude ±50 ft, heading ±10°, airspeed +5/−0 kt, bank ±5°. Mike: slow flight to specific headings; checklists before and after each maneuver.
Recognize and recover promptly at the stall; heading ±10°, bank as specified; no secondary stall.
Max-performance climbing 180° turn; 30° bank, smooth pitch change; roll out at minimum controllable airspeed ±10° heading.
Below Va, 45° bank, recover at the first indication, no excessive load factor.
50° ±5° bank, altitude ±100 ft, airspeed ±10 kt, rollout ±10°.
Correct configuration, bank, airspeed per POH; clearing; level-off.
Thinks while flying; uses checklist; stays ahead of the airplane.
Minimum ground speed at touchdown, keep weight off the nosewheel, proper flap/power.
Touchdown at or within 100 ft beyond the point, stabilized approach, max braking as appropriate.

Touchdown at or within 200 ft beyond the specified point. Steve’s big one: hit your point and be confident. Steve: simulated engine out; he tells you exactly what he wants. You have to make the airport. Hit the 1,000-footers and it counts as the power-off 180; if not, go around.
Lazy eights, steep spirals, eights on pylons.
Not on the gouge but in the ACS. Know the standards for each. Steve: eights on pylons.
Short-field landing, full stop, then straight into a short-field takeoff.
Stop, configure per POH, short-field takeoff.
Simulated jammed trim, then a soft-field landing.
Fly with control forces; soft field: hold the nosewheel off as long as possible.

sections.intro: Eric started with the applicant’s knowledge test deficiencies, then went through the FOIs. He wants aviation scenarios and real student examples, not definitions.
qs: Human needs (Maslow). Give me an example with a student.
Physiological, security, belonging, esteem, cognitive & aesthetic, self-actualization. Lower needs must be met first: a hungry, tired or scared student won’t learn.
Defense mechanisms. What would one look like in a flight student?
Repression, denial, compensation, projection, rationalization, reaction formation, fantasy, displacement. E.g. student blames the wind for every bad landing (rationalization).
Perceptions and insights. What affects perception?

Physical organism, basic need, goals and values, self-concept, time and opportunity, element of threat. Insight = grouping perceptions into meaningful wholes; instructor helps by relating parts to the whole.
Laws/principles of learning. Use aviation examples.
Readiness, exercise, effect, primacy, intensity, recency. E.g. primacy: teach the correct landing flow first; recency: review key points at the end of the lesson.
Source (sender), symbols (words, signs), receiver. Instructor must know the subject and the student’s background.
Lack of common experience, confusion between the symbol and the symbolized object, overuse of abstractions, interference (physiological, environmental, psychological).
Levels of learning (RUAC)? Where’s a student who can recite V-speeds but not use them?
Rote, understanding, application, correlation. That student is at rote.

Other FOIs (skimmed): memory and forgetting, transfer of learning, teaching methods, assessment, critique, lesson plans, motivation, learning plateaus, instructor responsibilities and professionalism.
Know each well enough to explain with an example.

sections.intro: The longest part of Eric’s oral. Scenario: Hank left for the airlines and handed you his “checkride-ready” private student. You find 3 hours of instrument training missing. Prove the student is eligible before you sign. Use AC 61-65 and the FAR/AIM.
qs: Hank says his private student is checkride ready. What do you do before signing anything?

Review every logbook entry yourself against Part 61: ground training (61.105), flight proficiency (61.107), aeronautical experience (61.109), knowledge test, prior endorsements. You’re the one signing.

40 hr total; 20 dual incl. 3 hr XC, 3 hr night (one 100 nm XC, 10 full-stop takeoffs/landings), 3 hr instrument, 3 hr test prep within 2 calendar months; 10 hr solo incl. 5 hr solo XC, one 150 nm XC with full-stop landings at 3 points (one leg >50 nm), 3 takeoffs/landings at a towered airport.
You find 3 hours of instrument training missing. Now what?
Student isn’t eligible. Provide (and log) the 3 hr of instrument training, then re-check everything before endorsing.
What endorsements does the student need for the practical test? Where are they?

Knowledge test (or pass report), and practical test endorsements: 3 hr prep within the preceding 2 calendar months and ready for the test, plus deficient knowledge test areas reviewed. Exact wording in AC 61-65 Appendix A.
Endorsements leading up to it (solo, solo XC, Class B, etc.)?
Pre-solo knowledge test and flight training, solo (90 days), solo XC (each flight and the general one), Class B/towered, etc. Look them up in AC 61-65 instead of memorizing.
What must you log and keep as an instructor?
Sign the student’s logbook for each lesson (61.189(a)); keep a record of endorsements you give and the results for 3 years (61.189(c)).

sections.intro: Eric asked how a CFI stays current. Know the FIRC option and the IACRA application/sign-off process. Note the Dec 2024 rule change below.
qs: How does a CFI stay current?

Since Dec 1, 2024 CFI certificates don’t expire; you need recent experience every 24 calendar months (61.197): pass a practical test for an additional instructor rating, a record of training (5 applicants endorsed with an 80% first-time pass rate), check airman/chief instructor duties, an FAA-sponsored proficiency program (15 activities), or a FIRC within the 3 calendar months before the end month.
What if your recent experience lapses?
Lapsed by no more than 3 calendar months: reinstate by completing a FIRC (61.199). Longer: practical test.
How do you apply after a FIRC?
Apply through IACRA with the FIRC graduation certificate; know who signs it off.

sections.intro: Have a risk management lesson plan or slideshow ready (Eric really liked one). Apply each acronym to a scenario. He likes the FAA Risk Management Handbook.
qs: Teach me risk management. (Lesson plan / slideshow ready.)
Objective, elements, scenario, completion standards. Uses the Risk Management Handbook.
Hazard: a condition or event that could cause harm. Risk: the likelihood and severity of a hazard’s outcome (risk matrix).
PAVE, 3P, CARE, TEAM: what are they and how do you use them?

PAVE (Pilot, Aircraft, enVironment, External pressures) to identify hazards. 3P (Perceive, Process, Perform). CARE (Consequences, Alternatives, Reality, External factors) to assess. TEAM (Transfer, Eliminate, Accept, Mitigate) to control.
5P: Plan, Plane, Pilot, Passengers, Programming (check at key points of flight). FRAT: flight risk assessment tool that scores risk before a flight.
ADM and SRM: hazardous attitudes, DECIDE, situational awareness?
5 hazardous attitudes and antidotes (anti-authority, impulsivity, invulnerability, macho, resignation). DECIDE model. SRM: risk, task, automation management, situational awareness, CFIT awareness.

sections.intro: Have a runway incursion lesson plan or slideshow ready.
qs: Lesson plan ready: definition, causes, signs, markings, taxi procedures, hot spots, situational awareness.

Mandatory (red/white: runway holding position, ILS critical area, no entry), location (black/yellow), direction (yellow/black), destination, information, runway distance remaining. Hold-short markings: solid lines on the taxiway side.
Explicit runway crossing clearances are required; read back all hold-short instructions; use progressive taxi if unsure; sterile cockpit while taxiing.
How do you keep situational awareness on the ground?
Review the airport diagram and hot spots before taxi, write down the taxi clearance, heads up, lights per AIM 4-3-23, ask ATC when unsure.

sections.intro: Eric had the applicant briefly teach Class G.
qs: Uncontrolled; surface up to the overlying Class E (700 or 1,200 AGL, or 14,500 MSL). Weather mins by day/night and altitude, the night pattern exception, no ATC communication required, traffic pattern rules at non-towered airports.

1,200 AGL or less: day 1 sm clear of clouds; night 3 sm, 500/1,000/2,000 (night pattern exception: 1 sm, clear of clouds within ½ mile of the runway). Above 1,200 AGL below 10,000 MSL: day 1 sm 500/1,000/2,000, night 3 sm. Above 1,200 AGL and 10,000 MSL: 5 sm, 1,000/1,000/1 sm.

sections.intro: The applicant taught eights on pylons. Know pivotal altitude, wind, entry, corrections and common errors.
qs: Objective, pylon selection (perpendicular to wind, ~½ mi apart), entry 45° to downwind between pylons at pivotal altitude, figure-8 with wingtip on the pylon.
What is pivotal altitude and how do you figure it?
Altitude where the wingtip line holds on the pylon: GS² ÷ 11.3 (knots) in feet AGL. Changes with groundspeed: highest downwind, lowest upwind.
How do you correct if the pylon moves?
Pylon moves ahead of the wingtip: you’re above pivotal altitude, descend. Pylon moves behind: climb. Don’t use rudder to hold it.
Using rudder to yaw the wing onto the pylon, poor pylon selection, bad entry, not anticipating altitude changes, uncoordinated flight, excessive bank, poor collision avoidance.

sections.intro: Standard opening. Have the logbook, knowledge test report (FOI if needed, IFI/instrument instructor test), endorsements and IACRA ready. Mike’s oral ran about an hour, then about an hour of flight.
qs: What do you need to be eligible for the CFII?

Commercial or ATP with an instrument rating; passed the instrument instructor knowledge test; endorsement from an authorized instructor on the fundamentals and instrument instruction areas; FOI test unless you already hold a CFI or exempt.
What are Parts 61, 71, 91, 95 and 97, and the AIM?

61 certification; 71 airspace (Part 75, jet routes and area high routes, was folded into 71); 91 operating rules; 95 IFR altitudes; 97 standard instrument procedures; AIM procedures and guidance (not regulatory).
What do you use the Instrument Flying Handbook for?
The FAA’s handbook on instrument flying and instrument instruction: instruments, attitude instrument flying, navigation, procedures.
Copy this CRAFT clearance (KHWD → KMRY via the HWD15 TEC route) and load it into ForeFlight. ETE and fuel required?
Read back CRAFT, find the TEC route, compute ETE and fuel: destination + alternate (if required) + 45 min.
Who needs a CFII (not just a CFI) to teach them?

Instrument training toward an instrument rating, a type rating not limited to VFR, and the instrument training required for the commercial certificate (61.195(c)). A CFI can give the private’s 3 hours of instrument training.
Can you give an IPC? What does it include and what do you sign?
Yes, as a CFII. Tasks from the Instrument Rating ACS (IPC table); log it and endorse per AC 61-65.
Can you log instrument time while teaching? When?
A CFII may log instrument time when conducting instrument flight instruction in actual instrument conditions. Simulated: the student logs it.
Limitations on instructing: hours per day, records you keep, how long?
No more than 8 hours of flight training in any 24 consecutive hours. Sign the student’s logbook for each lesson; keep endorsement records 3 years.
How do you stay current as a CFII?

Same CFI recent experience every 24 calendar months (61.197); to act as PIC under IFR you also need 61.57(c) currency. Since Dec 2024 CFI certificates don’t expire; a FIRC can reinstate if lapsed no more than 3 months (61.199).
Safety pilot vs instructor: who is PIC, who logs what?
Safety pilot is a required crewmember (91.109(c)); either can be PIC by agreement if qualified. When you instruct, you’re normally PIC; the student logs simulated instrument and dual received.

sections.intro: Expect the FOIs applied to instrument students, with real examples.
qs: Levels of learning applied to an instrument student?
Rote (recites the scan), understanding (knows why), application (flies a partial-panel approach), correlation (handles a new failure on an unfamiliar approach).
How do you prevent and fix scan fixation, omission and emphasis?
Teach a radial/selected scan centered on the attitude indicator; call out what the student missed; use partial panel to break fixation.
How do you teach the building-block approach to instrument training?
Basic attitude instrument flying → navigation → holds → approaches → full procedures → partial panel and scenarios.
A student hits a learning plateau on holds. What do you do?
Explain plateaus are normal, change the teaching method (draw it, sim, chair fly), break into smaller tasks, praise progress.
How do you assess an instrument student? Debrief?
Scenario-based, learner-centered grading; let the student self-assess first, then your critique: specific, objective, with a plan.
