Physiological issues you must teach under the hood: spatial disorientation and illusions?
Leans, Coriolis, graveyard spiral, somatogravic, inversion, elevator. Trust the instruments.

sections.intro: Know the instruments and how to teach control/performance vs primary/supporting.
qs: Control and performance method vs primary and supporting method?

Control instruments (attitude, power) set; performance instruments (altimeter, airspeed, heading, VSI) show the result. Primary/supporting: which instrument gives the most pertinent info for each axis during a maneuver.
Teach the required instruments one by one (have a lesson plan/slideshow covering them all).
Walk down the practical standards list of instruments: pitot-static, gyros, turn coordinator, HI/HSI/RMI, compass, ADF/VOR/DME/ILS, autopilot, transponder.
Teach straight-and-level, standard-rate turns, constant airspeed and constant rate climbs/descents.
Standard rate = 3°/sec; approx bank = (TAS ÷ 10) + 7. Pitch/power for performance.
Teach unusual attitude recovery. Common student errors?
Nose high: power in, nose down, wings level. Nose low: power out, wings level, nose up. Errors: pulling before leveling wings, fixating, slow recognition.
Partial panel: how do you teach it? How does the student recognize which instrument failed?
Cross-check for disagreement; cover failed instruments; fly with what’s left (G5/standby, turn coordinator, compass, timed turns).
Gyroscopic and pitot-static instruments: errors and failures, and how you’d explain them to a student.
Pitot blocked → ASI acts like altimeter; static blocked → frozen altimeter/VSI, alternate static. AHRS/vacuum failure symptoms. Mike: teach pitot-static and blockages.
Gyros: rigidity in space and precession. What are pendulous vanes?
Rigidity: a spinning gyro resists change in its plane. Precession: force acts 90° later in rotation. Pendulous vanes in a vacuum AI help keep the gyro erect.
What does a turn coordinator show that a turn-and-slip doesn’t?
Canted gyro, so it shows rate of roll as well as rate of turn (gouge: “rate of bank”). Turn-and-slip shows rate of turn only.
HI: heading gyro set to the compass. HSI: heading indicator combined with a CDI. RMI: needle pointing to the station on a slaved card.
Why reset the heading indicator about every 15 minutes?
Precession, including apparent drift from the earth’s rotation.
Draw two HSIs with the same deflection, one upside down. Which way do you go to intercept?

Answer in compass directions (turn north/south/east/west), not left/right. Mike will rant about reverse sensing and CFIs not teaching it right. An HSI never reverse-senses if the course is set correctly; a CDI does when flown backward.
Compass turns and timed turns: how do you teach them?
UNOS/ANDS; timed turns at standard rate (3°/sec). Mike: magnetic dip, and what’s done to reduce dip and turning errors (compass design/compensation).

sections.intro: Teaching procedures, not just flying them. Be ready to draw holds and brief a plate.
qs: Teach hold entries. Radial vs bearing in a hold clearance?
70° line: direct, parallel, teardrop. Radial is FROM the station; bearing is TO. Max speeds, leg timing.
Teach how to brief an approach plate.
Pilot briefing info, plan view, profile, minimums, airport sketch; top to bottom, set and verify.
Precision: ILS, PAR, GLS (DA). APV: LPV, LNAV/VNAV (DA). Non-precision: LP, LNAV, LOC, VOR, NDB (MDA).
DA: decide at that altitude; a momentary descent below while going missed is OK. MDA: level off and don’t go below without the 91.175 requirements.
LPV: WAAS vertical guidance, angular, DA. LNAV: lateral only, linear, MDA.
When can you descend below DA/MDA? Visual references?
91.175(c): continuously in position, flight visibility, one of the required references (100 ft rule on approach lights).
When is a procedure turn not flown?
NoPT, radar vectors to final, timed approach from a hold, or cleared straight-in.
Circling approach and missed approach from a circle.
Category speeds, protected area; lose sight → climbing turn toward the landing runway, then the missed.
DPs, ODPs, SIDs, climb gradients; how do you teach them?
200 ft/nm standard; fpm = ft/nm × GS ÷ 60. VCOA. Must you accept a SID?
GPS: RAIM/WAAS, annunciations, database currency, alternate planning.
TERM/LPV annunciation; check the AFMS for database and alternate rules.
How many satellites for 2D and 3D GPS position?
How many satellites for RAIM fault detection?
How many for fault detection and exclusion (FDE)?
Slant-range distance to the station, that’s all.
Teach the ILS in depth: where’s the FAF? Can your altimeter correct for nonstandard temperature? Marker beacons?

FAF = GS intercept at the published altitude, not the Maltese cross (that’s LOC only). Altimeter does not correct for temperature: cold temperature airport snowflake. OM ~FAF; MM ~CAT I DA; IM ~CAT II DA.
NDBs: calculate magnetic and relative bearing to the station with a fixed card, movable card and RMI.
MB = MH + RB (fixed card). Movable card/RMI: read the head of the needle.

Know what the transponder does (modes, altitude reporting). Autopilot limitations from the airplane’s autopilot AFMS supplement (pull it up). FMS: flight management system, integrates nav, performance and flight plan.
Why can you follow the GPS on the final segment of a VOR approach?
AIM 1-2-3: an RNAV system may be used on a VOR final if the underlying NAVAID is operational and monitored. Gouge: we have a backup CDI tuned to the VOR.

sections.intro: Scenario based; teach the student the decision, not just the rule.
qs: VMC: stay VFR and land. IMC: AVEF route, MEA altitude, leave clearance limit at EFC/ETA.
Icing and thunderstorms: how do you teach avoidance?
Visible moisture near/below freezing; AIRMET Zulu; exit icing; avoid storms by 20 nm.
Electrical/AHRS failure in IMC with a student: what do you do as the instructor?
Take the airplane if needed, declare, load shed, use backups, nearest VMC/approach.
What intake ice prevention does your airplane have?
Know your airplane: alternate air (automatic or manual) for fuel injected; carb heat for carbureted.
No. Prop boots are electrically heated (anti-ice). Wing/tail boots inflate (de-ice).
Anti-ice vs de-ice: which does your airplane have?
Anti-ice prevents ice from forming (heat, fluid). De-ice removes ice after it forms (boots). Know whether the airplane is approved for flight into known icing.
What keeps the fuel from freezing?
Avgas has a very low freezing point; the real issue is water in the fuel freezing, so sump it. Know the fuel vents and any heated components.
Why can you use onboard weather radar to avoid a storm but not FIS-B?
Onboard radar is real time. FIS-B NEXRAD is delayed (can be well over 10 min old): strategic only, never tactical.

sections.t: Flight portion (teach from the right seat)
sections.intro: Mike’s ~1 hr flight: he briefs it on the ground, then you teach the whole time. Keep talking. Mike loves the autopilot: use it as much as you want.
qs: Preflight lesson: brief what today’s lesson covers and its standards.
Objective, elements, completion standards; scenario. Mike: he briefs the whole flight on the ground first. Start up and go; no wasted time.
Instrument cockpit check and departure; teach as you go.
Taxi instrument checks, clearance, departure. Mike: you do checklists, RAIM/WAAS check, brief and tune the ILS; he does taxi and comms.
Teach straight-and-level under the foggles, then unusual attitudes (he recovers with a failed PFD).
Spot and correct errors promptly; explain.
You fly under the foggles to JOSIF while teaching him the autopilot.
Explain modes as you use them.
Teach recognition and flying on backups.
Teach entry, timing, wind correction; correct the student’s errors. Mike: hold planned on the ground, flown as the procedure turn at JOSIF to intercept the ILS.
Teach briefing, stabilized approach, DA decision. Mike: ILS to minimums, then a hard left turn for the missed; set up the RNAV instead. Brief RNAV, vectors, mins, missed hard left again.

MDA discipline, VDP, circling. Mike: back at 5,500 he takes the controls under foggles; you teach the VOR-A and give vectors. Don’t touch anything, just tell him what to do. Clear him for the approach before he intercepts. Missed heading 220.
Missed approach and loss of communications scenario.
Teach the published missed and 91.185 actions.
Learner self-assessment, critique, next lesson; correct logbook entry. Mike: he continues in, lands and taxis back while you teach.
Keep talking and teaching for the whole flight.
Say what you’re doing and why throughout.
What do you need to add a multiengine land class rating to your commercial certificate?

Training from an authorized instructor (an MEI) on the AMEL areas of operation, a logbook endorsement that you're prepared for the practical test, and passing the practical test. No knowledge test and no minimum hours are required for a class add-on.
Which endorsements do you need to act as PIC of the Baron?

Complex (retractable gear, flaps, controllable-pitch prop) under 61.31(e), and high-performance (more than 200 hp per engine) under 61.31(f). The IO-470s are 260 hp each, so both apply. Both are one-time endorsements.
What limitation do you get if you don't do the instrument tasks in the multiengine airplane?
"Airplane Multiengine VFR Only." To keep instrument privileges in multis, demonstrate the OEI instrument tasks (Area X, Tasks C and D) on the checkride.
Commercial ACS, removal of the AMEL VFR-only limitation
What does the examiner need from you and the airplane on checkride day?

Photo ID, pilot certificate, medical, logbook with the required endorsements, a completed IACRA application, and the DPE fee. For the airplane: airworthiness and registration certificates, operating limitations (POH/AFM), weight and balance, and maintenance records showing inspections and ADs are current. Bring a view-limiting device for the instrument tasks.
Can you carry passengers in a multi right after the checkride? What about insurance?

Legally yes, once you hold the rating and the complex/high-performance endorsements, and meet 61.57 currency in airplanes. Insurance is separate: the school's policy usually sets dual and PIC minimums in type before you can fly it as PIC or carry people.
What inspections and documents must be current for N8145R?

Annual (and 100-hour if used for hire/flight instruction), transponder within 24 calendar months, ELT inspection within 12 months and battery, ADs complied with, static/altimeter within 24 months for IFR, VOR check within 30 days for IFR. Documents: ARROW (airworthiness, registration, operating limitations, weight and balance).

sections.intro: All speeds are knots IAS at 5100 lb from the POH. A few limits depend on serial number, so check yours.
qs: What is VMCA in the Baron, and how is it marked?
78 kts IAS (80 kts CAS, 92 mph). The placard says MIN CONTROL SPEED SINGLE ENGINE 80 KTS. It's the red radial.
100 kts IAS (101 kts CAS / 116 mph on the ASI). One-engine-inoperative best rate of climb and the en route climb speed.
91 kts. One-engine-inoperative best angle of climb.
What is VSSE and why does it exist?
84 kts. The intentional one-engine-inoperative speed: the slowest speed you may intentionally cut an engine in training. The POH prohibits in-flight engine cuts below 84 kts.
VNE 224 kts IAS (red line). VNO 183 kts IAS (top of green). VA 157 kts IAS at 5100 lb.
122 kts for TC-955 and later (or earlier serials with the gross weight kit); 113 kts on TC-371, TC-502 thru TC-954. Full flaps are 28°.
143 kts IAS for TC-371, TC-502 thru TC-1156; 153 kts IAS for TC-1157 thru TC-1607. Same speed for operating and extended.
Approach flaps down 90 kts, flaps up 97 kts. Balked landing climb 90 kts.
Cruise climb and turbulent air penetration speeds?
Cruise climb 122 kts. Turbulent air penetration 157 kts.
Emergency descent speed and best glide?
Emergency descent 153 kts. Max glide range 120 kts, props feathered, about 2 nm per 1,000 ft AGL.
Maneuvering to final 100 kts; final approach flaps down 90 kts.
What are the airspeed indicator arcs?
White 68–122 (full flap range), green 78–183, yellow 183–224, red line 224, blue line 100 (IAS values; the ASI itself is marked in CAS).
5100 lb takeoff/landing, 5121 lb ramp (TC-955 and later or with Kit 55-4014); 5000/5021 lb on earlier B55s.
Main cabin compartment 400 lb, extended aft compartment 120 lb, nose compartment 300 lb (270 lb on earlier serials).
Aft limit 86 in aft of datum at all weights. Forward limit 74 in at 3800 lb and below, moving to 81.0 in at 5100 lb (TC-955+). Datum is 83.1 in forward of the forward jack points.
Normal category, flaps up: +4.4 G; the POH lists the negative limit as 3.0 G. Acrobatic maneuvers, including spins, are prohibited.
Continental IO-470-L, 260 hp at 2625 rpm. Takeoff/max continuous: full throttle, 2625 rpm. Max CHT 460°F, max oil temp 225°F, min takeoff oil temp 75°F, oil pressure 30 psi min (idle), 80 psi max.
Gauge ranges: oil, fuel pressure, MP, RPM, CHT?
Oil temp green 75–225°F. Oil pressure green 30–60 psi. Fuel pressure 1.5 min, green 5–17, cruise 5–9.5, 17.5 max. MP green 15–29.6, red 29.6 in. RPM green 2000–2625, red 2625. CHT green 200–460°F.
Don't crank more than 30 seconds; the normal procedures say no more than 30 seconds in any 4-minute period. Let it cool.

Take off and land on the mains only. Don't take off with gauges in the yellow arc or less than 13 gal in each main. Crossfeed only in an emergency in level flight. Slips/skids limited to 20 s (unbaffled tanks) or 30 s (baffled tanks or reservoirs).
One pilot minimum; one pilot plus five passengers.
Is the Baron approved for flight into known icing?
No. The ice protection hasn't been demonstrated to meet the known-icing requirements; exit icing as soon as possible if ice accumulates.

sections.intro: Know these cold. They come up on every multi oral.
qs: The minimum calibrated airspeed at which you can maintain directional control when the critical engine suddenly fails, with the other engine at takeoff power, and hold straight flight with no more than 5° of bank.
What are the certification conditions for VMC (the 'and stuff')?

Max takeoff power on the operating engine; critical engine windmilling (not feathered); most unfavorable (aft) CG; max takeoff weight (or less, as it's worst); gear up; flaps in takeoff position; cowl flaps in takeoff position; trimmed for takeoff; out of ground effect; sea level standard; up to 5° bank toward the good engine.
How does each factor change VMC? (density altitude, weight, CG, bank, prop, gear, flaps)

Higher density altitude: VMC decreases (less power). Aft CG: increases (shorter rudder arm). Heavier: decreases. Bank toward the good engine (up to 5°): decreases. Windmilling prop: increases; feathered: decreases. Gear down: decreases (keel effect). Flaps down: generally decreases. More power: increases.
What is the critical engine and what makes it critical? (PAAT)

The engine whose failure most hurts performance and control. P-factor, Accelerated slipstream, Spiraling slipstream, Torque. On a conventional twin (both turning clockwise), the left engine is critical.
Why bank into the good engine?

With wings level and ball centered you're in a sideslip toward the dead engine. A few degrees of bank toward the operating engine (2–5°, ball about half out toward the good engine) gives zero sideslip, the least drag and best climb, and lowers VMC.
What happens to performance when you lose an engine?
You lose 50% of power but about 80% or more of your climb performance, because climb comes from excess power. Drag also rises from the windmilling prop, sideslip and rudder deflection.
Why is VMC dangerous at high density altitude?
VMC goes down with altitude while stall speed stays the same, so they can meet; above that altitude you may stall before reaching VMC, which can cause a spin.
VMC demonstration: entry, what you watch for, and recovery?

Above 5000 ft AGL (POH), gear and flaps up, props high rpm, above 84 kts. Simulated dead engine idle, other engine max MP. Slow about 1 kt per second holding heading with rudder and 5° bank into the good engine. At the first sign of VMC (can't hold heading) or a stall warning: reduce power on the operating engine to idle and lower the nose, then recover. Within 20° of heading (ACS).
Baron B55 POH Sec 4; ACS CA.X.B
Define VSSE, VYSE, VXSE and why each matters.

VSSE (84): slowest speed to intentionally fail an engine in training. VYSE (100, blue line): best single-engine rate; most altitude per time or least sink. VXSE (91): best single-engine angle, for obstacles.
Baron B55 POH Sec 3; AFH Ch 12
What is single-engine service ceiling vs absolute ceiling?
Service: altitude where you can still climb 50 fpm on one engine (feathered). Absolute: where single-engine climb is zero. Example from the POH chart: 9,000 ft at 4,550 lb and 5°C.

Accelerate-stop: accelerate to lift-off speed, lose an engine, stop. Accelerate-go: accelerate, lose an engine, continue the takeoff and climb to 50 ft. Use the POH charts; on most runways the accelerate-go can be very long or impossible.
What is zero thrust and how do you set it in the Baron?

A setting on the 'failed' engine that gives about the same drag as a feathered prop, so you can practice without shutting it down. Alternately retard the prop and throttle: prop lever to the feather detent, throttle to 12 in. MP.
What's the 'zone of decision' after takeoff?

Before gear up with a usable runway: close both throttles and land straight ahead. After gear up, if you can climb at VYSE: fly the engine-failure flow. If you can't climb: land on the best available area under control rather than stalling or losing VMC.
Why maintain VYSE, and when would you go slower?
Best climb or least sink on one engine. Only slower for obstacles (VXSE, 91 kts). Never below VMC (78 kts); if you get slow, reduce power on the good engine.
What's the danger of a windmilling prop and why feather fast?
A windmilling prop makes huge drag and raises VMC. Feather quickly, before rpm drops toward the anti-feather lock speed.

Control column full forward, full rudder opposite the spin, power to idle on both engines (nearly simultaneously), ailerons neutral; hold until rotation stops, then neutralize and pull out smoothly. Spins aren't approved and weren't tested.
How do you find zero sideslip in the airplane?

Bank about 2–3° toward the operating engine and let the ball sit about half its width toward the operating engine. A yaw string on the windshield centered is the precise indication. The exact bank varies with airspeed and power.
Why do you lose directional control below Vmc?

The rudder's effectiveness depends on airflow (dynamic pressure). As you slow, the rudder can no longer generate enough yawing moment to balance the asymmetric thrust of the operating engine, so the airplane yaws and rolls toward the dead engine.
What drag items hurt OEI performance the most, in order?
Windmilling prop (largest), then extended gear and flaps, then sideslip from flying uncoordinated, then an open cowl flap on the dead engine. Feather, clean up, fly zero sideslip.

sections.intro: How the IO-470s, props and fuel system work. Expect to draw the fuel system.
qs: Two Continental IO-470-L: fuel injected, air cooled, six cylinder, horizontally opposed, 260 hp each at 2625 rpm. Normally aspirated.
Is the Baron's critical engine the left or right? Why?

Both engines turn clockwise (as seen from behind), so the left engine is critical: losing it leaves the right engine, whose descending blade (P-factor) has the longer arm from the centerline. Also PAAT: P-factor, Accelerated slipstream, Spiraling slipstream, Torque.
How do the props work? What makes them feather?

Constant speed, full feathering, hydraulically controlled. Oil pressure (boosted by the governor) moves the blades to low pitch / high rpm. Springs and counterweights move them to high pitch and feather. Lose oil pressure and the prop goes toward feather.
Why don't you pull the prop lever past the detent during the runup?

Past the detent the prop goes rapidly to full feather, which puts high stress on the blade shanks and engine. Exercise in the governing range only (2200 rpm); feather check is a separate step at 1500 rpm.
Can the prop feather after the engine stops? Why does it matter?

Many props have anti-feathering lock pins that engage below about 800 rpm, so you must feather before rpm decays that far. That's why you feather promptly. Check your prop's supplement (Hartzell/McCauley).
How do you unfeather in flight?
With unfeathering accumulators: prop control full forward (starter briefly if needed). Without: prop forward of the detent to mid-range and engage the starter. Follow the AIR START checklist.

Each wing has a main tank in the leading edge (22 gal standard, 37 gal optional) and a 31-gal auxiliary tank outboard of the nacelle: 106 gal usable standard, 136 optional. Each engine has its own selector (MAIN, AUX, CROSSFEED, OFF); vapor return goes back to the tank in use. 8 drains.
What does the fuel pressure gauge actually measure?

Metered fuel pressure at the injection manifold valve, not engine-driven or boost pump pressure. It's used as a fuel flow indicator for leaning; the green sectors are 45–75% power, lower edge normal lean, upper edge best power.
How do the boost pumps work and when do you use them?

Two-speed electric (HIGH/LOW). HIGH: priming before start, or if the engine-driven pump fails. LOW: in high ambient temps (90°F+) for ground ops, takeoff and climb, and for crossfeed. Don't use HIGH with the engine running normally; it's more pressure than the injectors accept at reduced power.
How does crossfeed work? Why can't both selectors be on crossfeed?

Either engine can draw from the opposite side's tanks for emergencies in level flight. A mechanical interlock keeps both selectors off CROSSFEED at once because that would cut fuel to both engines. Not for balancing fuel.
Walk me through crossfeeding with the left engine dead.
1 Right boost pump LOW. 2 Left selector MAIN or AUX (the tank you want to use). 3 Right selector CROSSFEED. 4 Right boost pump LOW or OFF as needed.
Why must the fuel selectors sit in the detents?
Placard: NO FUEL FLOW TO ENGINES BETWEEN DETENTS.
Induction system: what if the air filter clogs?
A spring-loaded alternate air door on the plenum opens automatically and the engine runs on alternate air from inside the nacelle.
Full pressure, wet sump, 12 quarts each. A thermostatic bypass controls cooler flow. Dipsticks are calibrated per engine (canted engines), so they're not interchangeable.
How do you lean with the EGT?
Lean to peak and note where it starts to fall. Cruise (lean): enrich to 25°F rich of peak. Best power: 100°F rich of peak. Run 25°F or more rich of peak only; recheck after power or altitude changes.
Max cruise 24.5 in / 2450 rpm. Recommended 24.0/2300 and 22.0/2200. Economy 20.0/2100. Cruise climb 25 in (or full throttle) / 2500 rpm.
Cowl flaps: how are they controlled?
Electric, one switch per engine on the pilot's subpanel: up = closed, down = open. An amber light shows when either is open. Open for ground ops and climb, closed in descent.

sections.intro: Know these well enough to draw them.
qs: 24-volt, single-wire, negative ground. A 24-volt, 17 amp-hour battery (or two 12-volt 25 Ah in series) under the nose baggage floor. Two 24-volt, 50-amp belt-driven alternators (early ones had 25-amp generators) with loadmeters showing percent load.
Two transistorized voltage regulators; only one works at a time, the other is standby, chosen with a selector switch.
One ALT OUT light comes on. What do you do?
Check that alternator's loadmeter. No load: turn the affected alternator off and manage the load (max 1.0 on the remaining loadmeter).
Overvoltage light or both ALT OUT lights?

Check the loadmeters. No load = regulator failure: switch regulators. If it recurs, return to the original regulator and reduce load. If both alternator circuits have failed: both ALT switches off and minimize load, you're on battery only.
After start, the loadmeters total more than .2 after 2 minutes. Now what?
With no extra equipment on at 1000–1200 rpm and no sign of decreasing, it's an electrical malfunction. Battery and alternator switches off; don't take off.

Battery and alternator switches OFF (electric instruments go out), oxygen as required, all electrical switches OFF, then battery and alternators back ON and essential equipment on one at a time to isolate the bad item. Cabin heat off, cabin air pushed in, storm window if needed.
What powers the gyros? What if a vacuum pump fails?

Two engine-driven vacuum pumps feed one system. If one fails, check valves close and the other runs all the gyros. Red buttons on the suction gauge show which source failed. Normal suction 4.8–5.25 in Hg (or 3.75–5.25 depending on gauge).

Electric motor drives an actuator under the front seats through linkage. Two-position switch (pull out of the detent). Red light = up, green = down, only at full travel; a mechanical nose gear pointer shows transit. A squat switch on the main strut opens the circuit on the ground, but never rely on it.
When does the gear warning horn sound?
Intermittently when either throttle is pulled back below a setting that would sustain two-engine flight with the gear up. On one engine you can silence it by advancing the dead engine's throttle.
How do you extend the gear manually?

Slow down. LDG GR MOTOR breaker PULL, gear handle DOWN, engage the handcrank behind the front seats and turn counterclockwise about 50 turns, check the mechanical indicator (and lights if you have power). Never retract manually or run the motor with the crank engaged.
You extended the gear for a real emergency. Anything after landing?
Don't move any gear controls or reset breakers until the airplane is on jacks; the failure may be in the up circuit and the gear could retract on the ground.
Electric, three-position switch (pull out of the detent). Full down is 28°. You get 10° and 20° by returning the switch to OFF when the mark lines up (or a dial indicator on TC-1011 and later).

Hydraulic, toe brakes on the main wheels; reservoir in the nose baggage area. Parking brake: pull the control and pump the pilot's pedals. Don't hold one side's pedals while the other side pumps; you can lose braking on that side. Use chocks, not the parking brake, for long parking.

Pitot under the left wing (optional right for the copilot). Static ports on each side of the aft fuselage. Alternate static selector on the lower sidewall by the pilot, pulling from inside the cabin. Use the PERFORMANCE section corrections.
How does the stall warning work? Is it heated?

A vane on the left wing leading edge triggers a horn. The vane and plate are heated by the PITOT HEAT switch. It doesn't work with the battery and alternators off. With ice on the airplane, don't trust it.
Cabin heater: what kind, and what are its quirks?

Combustion heater in the nose (it burns fuel; drain its fuel strainer on preflight). Overheat thermostat blows a fuse; fix the cause before using it again. The heater won't run if CABIN AIR is pulled more than halfway. The blower only runs with the gear down.
The middle window on each side: lift the latch, pull the release pin, push the window out. Door unlatched in flight: it trails 3–4 inches open, handling is fine, return and land normally.
What ice protection does the Baron have, and can you go into icing?

Depending on equipment: pneumatic surface deice boots, electrothermal prop deice (or fluid anti-ice), pitot heat, heated stall warning, heated fuel vents, alternate static and alternate air. Not approved for known icing; exit as soon as ice accumulates.
How do the surface deice boots work?

Engine-driven pump pressure inflates the boots for 5–6 seconds per AUTO cycle, then vacuum holds them down. Either engine supplies enough pressure. Wait for 1/2 to 1 inch of ice; cycling too early can cause bridging. Pressure 9–20 psi while inflating. Stall speeds go up about 4 kts with the boots operating.
Boots fail on AUTO, or won't deflate?
Failed AUTO: switch to MANUAL (boots inflate only while held, no more than 8 seconds). Won't deflate: pull the deice circuit breaker.
How does electrothermal prop deice work?

Heated boots on each blade, cycled by a timer. Ammeter 7–12 amps (2 blade) or 14–18 amps (3 blade). Don't run it with the props stopped. Relieve imbalance by briefly increasing rpm. Turn it off while running the heater blower or gear motor if on one alternator.
Check the breaker; wait about 30 s before resetting. Still zero: turn it off and consider it inoperative. More than 15 A (2 blade) / 23 A (3 blade): don't use it unless the need is urgent.
Bottle of 38–66 cu ft (nose baggage or aft cabin), 1850 psi full. Plug the mask in to start flow; unplugging stops it. Figure duration from the chart times percent full. No smoking.

sections.intro: Say these in order. The Flows tab drills the exact steps.
qs: How do you identify which engine failed?

Dead foot, dead engine: rudder pressure is on the good engine's side. Verify by partially retarding the suspected throttle: no change in sound or control pressure means you have the right one. Don't use the tach or MP; they can read near normal.
Engine failure during the takeoff roll?
Throttles closed, maximum braking. If you can't stop on the runway: fuel selectors OFF, battery, alternators and magnetos OFF.
Engine failure after lift-off: POH steps?

Gear and flaps UP; throttle (dead engine) CLOSED; prop (dead engine) FEATHER; power (good engine) as required; hold the speed you had at the failure (100 kts max) until clear of obstacles. Then secure: mixture idle cut-off, fuel selector off, boost pump off, magnetos off, alternator off, cowl flap closed. Monitor electrical load (max 1.0).
Is continued flight after an engine failure on takeoff guaranteed?

No. The POH says an immediate landing is advisable regardless of weight; continued flight can't be assured above the weight from the TAKE-OFF WEIGHT graph, and you'll lose altitude while cleaning up and feathering.
Below 78 kts with an engine out?
Reduce power on the operating engine as needed to keep directional control. Control comes before climb.
Mixtures idle cut-off, keep cranking the affected engine, fuel selectors OFF, battery and alternators OFF, use the extinguisher.
Fuel selector OFF, mixture idle cut-off, prop FEATHER, boost pump OFF, magnetos OFF, alternator OFF on the affected engine. Land immediately using single-engine procedures.
Props 2625 rpm, throttles closed, 153 kts, gear down, flaps 10°.
Props feathered, flaps up, gear up, cowl flaps closed, 120 kts. About 2 nm per 1,000 ft.
When sure you'll make the field: gear down, flaps as required, 90 kts, power to hold about 800 fpm descent. When there's no chance of a go-around: flaps down and land normally.
Power max allowable, gear up, flaps up, 100 kts. Don't attempt it once the flaps are fully extended; level flight may not be possible at some weights and temperatures.

Fuel selector MAIN or AUX, throttle about 1/4 travel, mixture full rich (half travel above 5,000 ft), boost pump LOW, magnetos ON, unfeather (prop forward; starter if needed), then adjust controls, boost pump off, alternator on, check oil pressure, warm up at 2000 rpm / 15 in. Figure out why it failed first.
Cowl flaps closed, wing flaps as desired, throttles closed, fuel selectors off, mixtures idle cut-off, battery, alternators and magnetos off, wings level, get out quickly. Firm sod if possible.
Emergency static air source OPEN (lower sidewall by the pilot); use the alternate static calibration charts. Keep it closed when not needed.

Fly first: pitch for blue line, rudder to stop the yaw, bank 2–3° toward the good engine. Mixtures, props, throttles forward. Flaps up, gear up. Identify: dead foot, dead engine. Verify: slowly retard the suspected throttle; no change confirms it. Feather that prop. Then secure the dead engine (mixture cutoff, mags off, fuel off, boost pump off, alternator off, cowl flap closed), and run the checklist.
N8145R POH Section 3; Airplane Flying Handbook ch. 13

Normal takeoff on runway __, Vr __, blue line __. Engine failure before rotation, or with gear down and runway remaining: throttles closed, stop straight ahead. Failure after liftoff with gear up and a positive climb: blue line, identify, verify, feather, return or continue. If I can't climb, land straight ahead under control.
An engine fails right after liftoff. What decides whether you continue?

Airspeed, configuration, runway remaining and performance. If the gear is still down and runway remains, close the throttles and land. If the gear is up, you're at or above blue line and the airplane can climb on one engine at that weight and density altitude, continue with the flow. If it can't climb, land under control as nearly straight ahead as possible.
Commercial ACS IX.F; Airplane Flying Handbook ch. 13
When would you NOT feather right away?

When altitude and time allow troubleshooting, such as a partial power loss at cruise: check fuel selectors, boost pumps, mixtures, mags, alternate air. A partially working engine may still help. Near the ground on takeoff or go-around, you don't troubleshoot; identify, verify, feather.
Engine fails on short final. Go around or land?
Land. A single-engine go-around low and slow, with gear and flaps out, may not be possible. Plan OEI approaches to make the go-around decision early, and once committed, land.
What happens if you lose oil pressure on one engine?

The prop moves toward feather because governor oil pressure holds it in low pitch, and the engine will fail soon. Treat it as an impending engine failure: identify, verify, feather and secure before the prop locks out or the engine seizes.
Why do training engine cuts happen at or above Vsse instead of near Vmc?

Vsse gives a margin above Vmc and stall so a slow reaction or a real problem during training doesn't lead to loss of control. Instructors simulate failures by pulling a throttle (or mixture only at altitude/per school policy), never below Vsse in flight.

Boost pumps off (LOW if 90°F+), instruments, fuel on mains, mixtures rich or as required, props exercised at 2200, loadmeters, 1700 rpm mag check (150 rpm max drop, 50 rpm max difference), 1500 rpm feather check (don't let it drop more than 500 rpm), idle, friction, trim, flaps, controls, doors and windows, parking brake off.

Takeoff power before brake release (full throttle, 2625 rpm, mixture set to the fuel pressure for the altitude). Accelerate to lift-off (84) and 50-ft speed (91). Gear up with a positive rate and no runway left to land on. Climb speed when clear of obstacles.
If the engine is hot and it's 90°F or more: mixture idle cut-off, boost pump HIGH for 30–60 s, then OFF, mixture full rich, then normal start.
Mixture idle cut-off, throttle open, crank to clear; as it starts, throttle to idle and mixture full rich.
External power start: which engine first?
Right engine first; disconnect external power before starting the left. Alternators off when connecting; battery on. APU set to 27.0–28.5 volts.
25 psi within 30 seconds. Warm up at 800–1200 rpm; don't go above 1200 until oil is 75°F.
Parking brake, props high rpm, throttles 1000 rpm, boost pumps off, electrical and avionics off, mixtures idle cut-off, magnetos off after the engines stop, battery and alternators off, control lock.
Max 172 kts in smooth air, 157 kts in rough air. Cowl flaps closed, mains selected, avoid long idle descents (shock cooling, low CHT).
What do you use to figure single-engine climb performance for today?

The POH Section 5 'Climb – One Engine Inoperative' and 'Service Ceiling – One Engine Inoperative' charts, and the Take-Off Weight / accelerate-stop / accelerate-go charts. Brief whether you can climb on one engine at today's weight and density altitude before takeoff.
Do a weight and balance for today.

Use the airplane's actual empty weight and moment, add people, baggage (watch the 400/120/300 lb limits) and fuel (6 lb/gal), check against 5100 lb and the CG envelope (74–86 in). Check at takeoff and landing weights.
It's a hot summer day at Ogden (field ~4,470 ft). How do you decide whether to take off?

Compute density altitude, then single-engine climb rate and service ceiling at your weight, accelerate-stop vs runway length, and obstacle clearance. If an engine failure after liftoff wouldn't give a positive climb, brief that a failure before a safe altitude means landing ahead or reducing weight. Consider leaving fuel or passengers, or waiting for cooler temperatures.
POH Section 5; Airplane Flying Handbook ch. 13
How do weight and CG affect the Baron's performance and control?

Heavier: longer takeoff, lower climb and single-engine ceiling, but lower Vmc. Aft CG: less stable, higher Vmc, better cruise. Forward CG: more stable, higher stall speed, heavier pitch forces on landing. Compute weight and balance for takeoff and landing with the actual fuel burn.
POH Section 6; Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge ch. 10

sections.intro: Commercial ACS tolerances for the AMEL add-on. Your examiner will pick the tasks.
qs: At a safe altitude (recover no lower than 3,000 ft AGL), gear up, flaps and cowl flaps as briefed, props high RPM. Slow to about Vsse + 10, idle the critical (left) engine, max power on the right. Raise the pitch to slow about 1 kt per second, holding heading with rudder and up to 5° bank. Recover at the FIRST sign of loss of directional control, stall warning or buffet: reduce power on the operating engine and lower the nose together, then accelerate to Vsse/Vyse and climb.
Commercial ACS X.B; Airplane Flying Handbook ch. 13

Fly the engine-failure flow, actually feather and secure the engine at a safe altitude, maneuver with turns in both directions (including toward the dead engine), then restart. Altitude ±100 ft, heading ±10°, airspeed ±10 kt; keep zero sideslip. Check exact tolerances in the ACS.
OEI by reference to instruments (straight and level, turns).

Under the view-limiting device, handle the failure with the flow, then hold altitude, heading and airspeed within standards and make standard-rate turns. Typical tolerances: altitude ±100 ft, heading ±10°, airspeed ±10 kt, bank ±5°.
Instrument approach with one engine inoperative.

Fly a published approach with the engine simulated feathered (zero thrust). Brief it, keep blue line on the intermediate and initial segments, extend gear at the FAF or glideslope intercept, and fly to instrument approach standards. Decide on a missed approach early; a single-engine missed may not be possible.
Commercial ACS X.D; Instrument Rating ACS
Normal, crosswind and short-field takeoffs and landings in the Baron.

Use POH speeds, briefing before every takeoff, gear up only when no usable runway remains and a positive climb shows. Short-field: max power before brake release, rotate at the POH speed, Vx to clear the obstacle, then Vy. Landing: stabilized, on speed, touchdown within the ACS point-and-distance standard for the task.
Commercial ACS IV.A, B, E, F
50° ±5° bank, 360° in both directions, altitude ±100 ft, airspeed ±10 kt, rollout heading ±10°. The Baron has heavier pitch forces than a single; trim and add power as needed.

Slow flight: altitude ±50 ft, heading ±10°, airspeed +5/−0 kt, bank ±5°. Power-off and power-on stalls: recognize and recover promptly at the stall, with symmetric power and coordinated controls; no secondary stall. Power-on stalls in a twin use reduced power per the POH or examiner.
Max power, pitch for Vx or Vy as needed, flaps to the POH go-around setting, gear up once a positive climb is established, then clean up the rest. Call it early and keep it coordinated.
Expect at least one: gear that won't extend (emergency extension), alternator failure, electrical failure, vacuum failure, rough engine. Use the checklist, verbalize, and keep flying first.
Establish VYSE (or VXSE / VMC+5 if obstacles), clean up, simulate feathering (evaluator sets zero thrust), secure, heading ±10°, airspeed ±5 kts.
Approach speed ±5 kts in landing configuration until landing is assured; touch down in the first third of the runway, no drift, on centerline.
